title: Mathematics · Grade 10 · Term 2: Geometry and functions · Set A
subject: Mathematics

questions.question: A triangle has angles 48° and 62°. Find its third angle.
questions.explanation: Interior angles total 180°: 180 − 48 − 62 = 70°. State the angle-sum reason in a written solution.

questions.question: Find the midpoint of A(2; 4) and B(8; 10).
questions.explanation: Average the x-coordinates and y-coordinates separately: ((2+8)/2; (4+10)/2).

questions.question: For f(x) = 2x + 3, what is f(−2)?
questions.explanation: Substitute with brackets: 2(−2)+3 = −4+3 = −1. A negative input does not always give a negative output.

questions.question: Which point lies on y = x²?
questions.explanation: Squaring means multiplying a number by itself: (−3)² = 9. The minus sign is inside the brackets.

questions.question: A straight line passes through (0; 3). Its intersection with y=x² has x-coordinates −1 and 3. Which equation fits all these conditions?
questions.explanation: The two intersections are (−1;1) and (3;9). Their gradient is (9−1)/(3−(−1))=2; the intercept is 3. Checking both points rejects the other lines.

title: Mathematics · Grade 10 · Term 3: Trigonometry, statistics and growth · Set A
subject: Mathematics

questions.question: A right triangle has opposite side 3 and hypotenuse 5 for angle θ. What is sin θ?
questions.explanation: Sine is opposite divided by hypotenuse. Identify the sides relative to θ before choosing a ratio.

questions.question: Find the median of 3, 7, 7, 10, 18.
questions.explanation: The ordered list has five values; the third is the median. The mean would be 9, a different measure.

questions.question: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue counters. One is chosen at random. P(blue) = ?
questions.explanation: There are 2 blue outcomes out of 5 equally likely counters. Probability is favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes.

questions.question: R2 000 earns 8% simple interest each year for 3 years. Find the final amount.
questions.explanation: Interest = 2 000 × 0.08 × 3 = R480. Add the original R2 000; R480 alone is only the interest.

questions.question: Five numbers have median 8 and mean 10. One number, 20, is replaced by 30 without changing the median. Which conclusion follows?
options: The mean stays 10; the median becomes 18.
The mean becomes 12; the median stays 8.
questions.explanation: The total increases by 10 while the count stays five, so the mean rises by 2. The stipulated unchanged median shows why the two averages respond differently.

title: Mathematics · Grade 10 · Term 4: Measurement and number-pattern revision · Set A
subject: Mathematics

questions.question: A closed cube has side length 4 cm. Find its total surface area.
questions.explanation: A cube has six square faces. Surface area = 6 × 4² = 96 cm²; 4³ gives volume instead.

questions.question: Find the nth term of 5, 8, 11, 14, …
questions.explanation: The common difference is 3, so use 3n + c. Setting n = 1 gives c = 2. Check n = 2 gives 8.

questions.question: A cylinder has radius 3 cm and height 5 cm. Find its volume in terms of π.
questions.explanation: Volume = πr²h = π × 3² × 5. Radius is squared; do not use the diameter as the radius.

questions.question: Expand (x + 4)(x − 2).
questions.explanation: Multiply all four pairs: x² − 2x + 4x − 8. Combine the middle terms to get 2x.

questions.question: A closed cube is enlarged until its volume is eight times the original. A learner says its surface area also becomes eight times as large. Which correction is justified?
options: Lengths become eight times as large, so area doubles.
Lengths double, so surface area is unchanged.
Lengths double, so surface area becomes four times as large.
Lengths quadruple, so surface area doubles.
questions.explanation: Volume scales with the cube of length: a factor of 8 means lengths double. Area scales with the square, giving a factor of 4, not 8.

title: Mathematics · Grade 11 · Term 2: Circle geometry, coordinates and functions · Set A
subject: Mathematics

questions.question: The angle at the centre of a circle is 100°. What is the angle at the circumference subtended by the same arc?
questions.explanation: The angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference on the same arc. Divide 100° by 2.

questions.question: Find the gradient of the line through (1; 2) and (5; 10).
questions.explanation: Gradient = change in y / change in x = (10−2)/(5−1) = 2. Use the same subtraction order in both differences.

questions.question: Where is the turning point of y = (x − 2)² + 3?
questions.explanation: In y = a(x−p)²+q the turning point is (p; q). The horizontal shift has the opposite sign to the bracket's constant.

questions.question: For y = 3/x + 1, which line is a horizontal asymptote?
questions.explanation: As the magnitude of x grows, 3/x approaches 0, so y approaches 1. x = 0 is the vertical asymptote.

questions.question: A parabola has turning point (2;−1) and passes through (0;7). Which equation satisfies both conditions?
questions.explanation: Write y=a(x−2)²−1. Substitution gives 7=4a−1, so a=2. The turning-point form and a second condition must both be used.

title: Mathematics · Grade 11 · Term 3: Trigonometric rules, probability and finance · Set A
subject: Mathematics

questions.question: Two sides of a triangle are 6 cm and 8 cm with included angle 30°. Find its area.
questions.explanation: Area = ½ab sin C = ½ × 6 × 8 × ½ = 12 cm². The stated angle must be between the sides used.

questions.question: A triangle has sides 5 and 7 with included angle 60°. Find the square of the opposite side.
questions.explanation: Cosine rule: c² = 5²+7²−2(5)(7)cos60° = 74−35 = 39. The question asks for c², not c.

questions.question: Events A and B are independent with probabilities 0.4 and 0.5. Find P(A and B).
questions.explanation: For independent events multiply: 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.20. Adding instead would not give the intersection.

questions.question: An asset of R10 000 depreciates by 10% annually on reducing balance. Value after 2 years?
questions.explanation: Use 10 000(0.9)² = 8 100. In year two the 10% applies to R9 000, not the original value.

questions.question: Independent events A and B have probabilities 0.4 and 0.5. A learner calculates P(A or B)=0.9. Which correction explains the error?
options: Independent means the overlap is zero, so 0.9 is correct.
questions.explanation: Independence gives P(A and B)=0.4×0.5=0.2; it does not mean mutually exclusive. The addition rule gives 0.4+0.5−0.2=0.7.

title: Mathematics · Grade 11 · Term 4: Patterns and measurement revision · Set A
subject: Mathematics

questions.question: Find the nth term of 2, 6, 12, 20, …
questions.explanation: The first differences are 4, 6, 8 and second difference is 2, so the quadratic coefficient is 1. Testing n²+n reproduces every term.

questions.question: A cone has radius 3 cm and perpendicular height 4 cm. Find its volume.
questions.explanation: V = ⅓πr²h = ⅓π × 9 × 4 = 12π cm³. Slant height is not used for volume.

questions.question: Simplify √50 in surd form.
questions.explanation: Factor 50 as 25×2, so √50 = √25 × √2 = 5√2. Only a perfect-square factor leaves the root.

questions.question: Solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0.
questions.explanation: Factor as (x−2)(x−3)=0. Either factor can be zero, giving two solutions.

questions.question: A cone and cylinder have equal radii. The cone must have the same volume as the cylinder. How must their perpendicular heights compare?
options: The cone's height must equal the cylinder's.
The cone's height must be one third of the cylinder's.
The cone's height must be three times the cylinder's.
The cone's height must be nine times the cylinder's.
questions.explanation: Equate ⅓πr²h_cone=πr²h_cylinder. Cancelling the common base area gives h_cone=3h_cylinder; compare formulas rather than the shapes' appearance.

title: Mathematics · Grade 12 · Term 2: Geometry and differential calculus · Set A
subject: Mathematics

questions.question: Find the gradient of the tangent to f(x) = x³ − 2x at x = 2.
questions.explanation: Differentiate first: f′(x)=3x²−2. Then f′(2)=12−2=10. f(2)=4 is the function value, not the gradient.

questions.question: A tangent touches a circle at A. What angle does it make with the radius to A?
questions.explanation: A radius drawn to a point of tangency is perpendicular to the tangent. Include the point-of-contact condition when citing the theorem.

questions.question: Find the equation of a circle with centre (2; −1) and radius 3.
questions.explanation: Use (x−a)²+(y−b)²=r². Here b=−1, so y−b becomes y+1, and r²=9.

questions.question: For f(x) = x² − 4x, where is the stationary point?
questions.explanation: At a stationary point f′(x)=0. Since f′(x)=2x−4, solve 2x−4=0 to get x=2.

questions.question: An open rectangular pen is built against a wall with 20 m of fencing for its other three sides. Which dimensions maximise its area?
options: 10 m perpendicular and 0 m along it
4 m perpendicular and 12 m along it
5 m perpendicular to the wall and 10 m along it
6 m perpendicular and 8 m along it
questions.explanation: With width x, length is 20−2x and area 20x−2x². Its derivative 20−4x vanishes at x=5; the negative second derivative confirms a maximum of 50 m².

title: Mathematics · Grade 12 · Term 3: Finance, regression and counting · Set A
subject: Mathematics

questions.question: R5 000 grows at 10% per year compounded annually. Its value after 2 years is…
questions.explanation: A=P(1+i)ⁿ = 5 000(1.10)² = 6 050. Compound interest includes interest on the first year's interest.

questions.question: A regression model is ŷ = 2x + 5. Predict y when x = 4.
questions.explanation: Substitute x=4: ŷ=2(4)+5=13. This is a model prediction, not a guaranteed observed value.

questions.question: How many 3-digit codes can be formed from 0–9 if repetition is allowed and a code may start with 0?
questions.explanation: Each of three positions has 10 choices. Multiply 10×10×10. A code differs from a three-digit number because leading zero is allowed.

questions.question: A test for a condition has P(positive and condition)=0.18 and P(positive)=0.30. Find P(condition given positive).
questions.explanation: Conditional probability divides the intersection by the conditioning event: 0.18/0.30 = 0.60.

questions.question: A regression fitted only to ages 12–18 predicts a person's height at age 80. Why should that prediction be treated cautiously?
options: A fitted line guarantees accurate predictions at every age.
The slope proves age is the only cause of height.
It extrapolates far beyond the observed ages, where the relationship may change.
questions.explanation: The model's observed age range is limited. A linear growth pattern during adolescence need not continue in adulthood, so substituting 80 does not validate the prediction.

title: Mathematics · Grade 12 · Term 4: Integrated examination revision · Set A
subject: Mathematics

questions.question: The first three terms of an arithmetic sequence are 7, 11, 15. Find term 20.
questions.explanation: Tₙ=a+(n−1)d = 7+19×4 = 83. There are 19 increases from term 1 to term 20.

questions.question: Find the derivative of f(x) = 2x³ − 5x² + 4.
questions.explanation: Apply the power rule term by term. A constant's derivative is zero; the exponent decreases by one.

questions.question: For x² − 4x + 3 = 0, what is the discriminant?
questions.explanation: Δ=b²−4ac = (−4)²−4(1)(3)=4. It is positive, so the quadratic has two distinct real roots.

questions.question: A circle has diameter AB with A(−2; 0), B(4; 0). Find its radius.
questions.explanation: Diameter length = 4−(−2)=6, so radius is half: 3. The centre is (1;0), but its x-coordinate is not the radius.

questions.question: A quadratic sequence has T₁=2, T₂=6 and T₃=12, with constant second difference 2. Which term is the first greater than 100?
questions.explanation: The sequence is Tₙ=n²+n. Solve n(n+1)>100 for positive integers: T₉=90 and T₁₀=110. Although later terms also exceed 100, the first is term 10.

title: Mathematical Literacy · Grade 10 · Term 2: Bills, units, scale and probability · Set A
subject: Mathematical Literacy

questions.question: A bill charges R50 fixed plus R2 per kWh. What does 80 kWh cost?
questions.explanation: Usage costs 80×R2 = R160. Add the fixed R50 once to get R210. A fixed charge is not multiplied by usage.

questions.question: Convert 2.5 litres to millilitres.
questions.explanation: One litre equals 1 000 millilitres. Multiply 2.5 by 1 000 and keep the unit.

questions.question: On a 1:100 plan, a wall measures 4 cm. Find its real length in metres.
questions.explanation: Multiply the drawing length by 100: 400 cm. Divide by 100 to convert centimetres to metres.

questions.question: A spinner has 8 equal sectors; 3 are green. P(green) is…
questions.explanation: Equal sectors give equally likely outcomes: 3 favourable sectors out of 8 total.

questions.question: Plan A costs R50+R2 per kWh; Plan B costs R90+R1 per kWh. At 30 kWh, which advice is justified?
options: Choose B because its unit charge is lower, regardless of usage.
Both cost R60 because only usage counts.
Choose A at R110 rather than B at R120 for this usage.
Choose A because it is cheaper at every usage.
questions.explanation: A costs 50+60=R110; B costs 90+30=R120. The fixed charge matters. At other usage levels the cheaper plan can change, so avoid an unrestricted claim.

title: Mathematical Literacy · Grade 10 · Term 3: Budgets, interest and floor plans · Set A
subject: Mathematical Literacy

questions.question: A learner earns R900 and spends R250 on transport and R400 on food. What remains?
questions.explanation: Total spending = 250+400 = R650. Remaining money = income−spending = 900−650 = R250.

questions.question: A savings example uses 5% simple annual interest on R1 200 for one year. Find the interest.
questions.explanation: 5% means 0.05. Interest = 1 200×0.05 = R60; R1 260 includes the original savings.

questions.question: A rectangular room is 4 m by 3 m. Find its floor area.
questions.explanation: Area = length×width = 4×3 = 12 m². 14 m is its perimeter, a length rather than an area.

questions.question: A product costs R80 and sells for R100. What is the profit?
questions.explanation: Profit = selling price−cost price = R100−R80 = R20. This is the amount, not a percentage.

questions.question: A learner has R900 income and R650 necessary expenses. A savings goal is R300. Which plan meets it without borrowing?
options: Keep expenses at R650 and save R300.
Increase expenses by R50 to reach the goal.
Reduce expenses by R50, leaving R300 to save.
Save the R900 and ignore expenses.
questions.explanation: Current surplus is R250, R50 below the goal. Expenses must fall to R600 or income rise by R50; savings cannot exceed the money left after expenses.

title: Mathematical Literacy · Grade 10 · Term 4: Data handling and year-end revision · Set A
subject: Mathematical Literacy

questions.question: Five taxi fares are R12, R15, R15, R18 and R20. Find the mode.
questions.explanation: The mode occurs most often. R15 appears twice; every other fare appears once.

questions.question: A class of 40 learners has 10 who walk to school. What angle represents them in a pie chart?
questions.explanation: The fraction is 10/40 = ¼. Multiply by 360° to get 90°. The percentage 25% is not an angle.

questions.question: A bar graph starts its vertical axis at 90 instead of 0. What should you check before comparing bars?
options: Whether every bar becomes a percentage
Whether the data must be false
Whether the shortened scale exaggerates differences
Whether the units can be ignored
questions.explanation: A truncated axis can make small differences look large. Read the scale and values before drawing a conclusion.

questions.question: A class survey asks only the top five achievers about study habits. What is a main limitation?
options: Five is always the correct sample size
The sample may not represent the whole class
questions.explanation: Choosing only high achievers introduces selection bias. Include learners with a range of experiences.

questions.question: Two adverts show the same sales rising from 100 to 110. One graph begins at zero; the other at 99. Which judgement is sound?
options: The second graph proves a 110% increase.
The first graph must conceal a fall.
Both can show correct values, but the second can exaggerate the visual increase.
Different axis starts necessarily mean different data.
questions.explanation: The numerical increase is 10/100×100=10% in both. The shortened axis changes visual proportions, so read the actual scale before judging the adverts.

title: Mathematical Literacy · Grade 11 · Term 2: Tax, tariffs and data · Set A
subject: Mathematical Literacy

questions.question: For this exercise, VAT is 15%. Find VAT on a price of R200 excluding VAT.
questions.explanation: VAT = 200×0.15 = R30. Add it for a VAT-inclusive price of R230. Use the rate provided in the question.

questions.question: A map uses 1:50 000. A route measures 6 cm. Find the actual distance.
questions.explanation: 6×50 000 = 300 000 cm = 3 000 m = 3 km. Convert units only after applying the scale.

questions.question: Find the range of 12, 15, 19, 21, 28.
questions.explanation: Range = maximum−minimum = 28−12=16. It describes spread, not the central value.

questions.question: A phone plan charges R100 plus R0.50 per minute. What is the total for 120 minutes?
questions.explanation: Variable cost = 120×0.50 = R60. Add the R100 fixed charge to get R160.

questions.question: A R200 pre-VAT item has a 10% discount before 15% VAT is added. A customer says the total is R205 by subtracting 10% and adding 15% of R200. What is correct?
options: R205, because both percentages use the original price.
R230, because a discount cannot change VAT.
R207, because VAT applies to the discounted R180.
R180, because VAT is already included.
questions.explanation: The discount is R20, leaving R180. VAT is 15% of R180, or R27. The final price is R207; the two percentage changes use different bases.

subject: Mathematical Literacy

questions.question: A stall has fixed costs R300, sells items for R20 and spends R5 per item. How many items break even?
questions.explanation: Each item contributes R20−R5 = R15 towards fixed costs. R300/R15 = 20 items; then total revenue equals total cost.

questions.question: A loan of R2 000 costs R150 interest and R50 in fees. Find the total repayment.
questions.explanation: Add principal, interest and fees: 2 000+150+50 = R2 200. Fees also affect borrowing cost.

questions.question: A design drawing uses 1:20. A table is 1.6 m long in real life. Find its drawing length in cm.
questions.explanation: Convert 1.6 m to 160 cm, then divide by 20. A reduced drawing is shorter than the real table.

questions.question: Actual spending is R3 600; the budget was R3 000. By what percentage did spending exceed the budget?
questions.explanation: The excess is R600. Divide by the original budget: 600/3 000×100 = 20%, not by actual spending.

questions.question: A stall's fixed costs are R300, selling price R20 and variable cost R5 per item. It can sell at most 18 items. Which conclusion follows?
options: It breaks even because revenue exceeds R300.
It cannot break even; 18 sales leave a R30 loss.
questions.explanation: At 18 sales revenue is R360, but costs are R300+R90=R390. The loss is R30. Contribution is R15 per item, requiring 20 sales to break even.

questions.question: A shop offers 20% off R450. What do you pay?

questions.question: Two fair coin tosses have outcomes HH, HT, TH, TT. P(exactly one head) = ?

questions.question: A box holds 6 L by its outside dimensions. A buyer needs to store 6 L of liquid and claims it is guaranteed to fit. Which response is justified?
options: The outside volume always equals usable liquid capacity.
Six litres means the box has a 6 m length.
Check internal capacity and usable space; outside dimensions do not guarantee 6 L storage.
questions.explanation: Capacity depends on internal dimensions, wall thickness and any necessary headspace. An external-volume calculation alone does not establish usable storage.

subject: Mathematical Literacy

questions.question: A rectangular floor is 6 m × 4 m. Tiles cover 0.25 m² each. Ignoring waste, how many tiles are needed?
questions.explanation: Floor area = 24 m². Divide by area per tile: 24/0.25 = 96. The units cancel to a count.

questions.question: A map distance of 7.5 cm represents 15 km. What is the map scale?
questions.explanation: 15 km = 1 500 000 cm. Divide both lengths by 7.5 to obtain 1:200 000.

questions.question: A cylindrical tank has radius 1 m and height 2 m. Using π = 3.14, find its capacity.
questions.explanation: V=πr²h = 6.28 m³. Multiply by 1 000 to convert cubic metres into litres.

questions.question: A bus leaves at 22:45 and arrives next day at 05:15. Find the journey time.
questions.explanation: From 22:45 to midnight is 1 h 15 min, then another 5 h 15 min. Add to get 6 h 30 min.

questions.question: A 24 m² floor needs 0.25 m² tiles. Add 10% to the tile count for waste; tiles come in packs of 10. How many packs must be bought?
questions.explanation: The basic count is 24÷0.25=96. With waste it is 105.6, requiring at least 106 tiles. Ten packs give only 100; eleven packs provide 110.

title: Mathematical Literacy · Grade 12 · Term 3: Plans, packaging and integrated practice · Set A
subject: Mathematical Literacy

questions.question: A floor plan uses 1:50. A door is 1.8 cm wide on the plan. Find the real width.
questions.explanation: Multiply 1.8 cm by 50 = 90 cm = 0.9 m. Retain the same units until after scaling.

questions.question: A carton holds 4 rows of 6 cans in one layer and has 3 layers. How many cans fit?
questions.explanation: Multiply rows × cans per row × layers: 4×6×3 = 72. Counting only one layer gives 24.

questions.question: A rectangular parcel is 40 cm × 30 cm × 20 cm. Find its volume.
questions.explanation: Multiply all three dimensions: 40×30×20 = 24 000 cm³. Adding lengths does not calculate volume.

questions.question: A delivery contract charges R250 plus R8 per kilometre. Find the cost for 35 km.
questions.explanation: The distance cost is 8×35 = R280. Add the fixed R250 once: R530.

questions.question: Contract A charges R250+R8/km; B charges R100+R12/km. A driver says B is always cheaper because its fixed charge is lower. What happens at 50 km?
options: B costs R700 and is R50 cheaper than A.
A costs R650 and is R50 cheaper than B.
A costs R400 because the fixed charge is ignored.
questions.explanation: A=250+8×50=R650. B=100+12×50=R700. A smaller fixed charge need not produce a smaller total once the distance charge is considered.

title: Mathematical Literacy · Grade 12 · Term 4: Exam revision: finance, data and probability · Set A
subject: Mathematical Literacy

questions.question: For this exercise, a price of R1 150 includes 15% VAT. Find the price before VAT.
questions.explanation: The inclusive price is 115% of the base. Divide R1 150 by 1.15. Subtracting 15% of R1 150 uses the wrong base.

questions.question: A salary rises from R8 000 to R8 600. Find the percentage increase.
questions.explanation: Increase = R600. Divide by original salary: 600/8 000×100 = 7.5%.

questions.question: A group has 12 learners; 7 are girls. One learner is selected fairly. P(not a girl) = ?
questions.explanation: There are 12−7=5 learners who are not girls. Use 5 favourable outcomes out of 12.

questions.question: A scatter plot shows that electricity use tends to rise with household size. What does this establish?
options: That every large household uses more than every small one
An association, not proof that size alone causes usage
That electricity use causes more household members
That other factors have no effect
questions.explanation: A trend describes association. Appliances, weather, income and behaviour can also affect use; correlation alone does not establish causation.

questions.question: An item costs R1 150 including 15% VAT. A shop removes VAT by deducting 15% of R1 150. Which judgement is correct?
options: The method is correct and gives R977.50 before VAT.
The method is wrong: divide by 1.15 to obtain R1 000.
The original price cannot be found from the information.
questions.explanation: The inclusive amount represents 115% of the pre-VAT base. Subtracting 15% of the inclusive amount uses a larger base than the original VAT calculation.

title: Physical Sciences · Grade 10 · Term 2: Electric circuits and atomic structure · Set A
subject: Physical Sciences

questions.question: A charge of 12 C passes a point in 4 s. Find the current.
questions.explanation: Current is charge per unit time: I=Q/Δt=12/4=3 A. Coulombs and seconds are not added.

questions.question: Two resistors of 2 Ω and 4 Ω are in series. Find the equivalent resistance.
questions.explanation: Series resistances add: R=2+4=6 Ω. The reciprocal formula applies to parallel resistors.

questions.question: A neutral atom has atomic number 11 and mass number 23. How many neutrons does it have?
questions.explanation: Mass number = protons + neutrons. Atomic number is protons, so neutrons = 23−11=12.

questions.question: Which statement describes isotopes of the same element?
options: Same mass number in every isotope
Same proton number, different neutron number
Different proton and electron numbers by definition
questions.explanation: The proton number identifies the element. Isotopes differ in neutrons and therefore in mass number.

questions.question: A learner investigates whether resistance depends on wire length but changes both length and thickness between trials. Which improvement best tests the claim?
options: Change thickness and material together at every length.
Use only one reading and assume a straight-line relationship.
Vary length while keeping material, thickness and temperature controlled.
Keep length fixed and change all other variables.
questions.explanation: Thickness, material and temperature can also affect resistance. Controlling them while changing length makes the comparison interpretable; repeated measurements improve reliability.

title: Physical Sciences · Grade 10 · Term 3: Motion and chemical equations · Set A
subject: Physical Sciences

questions.question: A learner walks 6 m east then 2 m west. Find the displacement.
questions.explanation: Take east positive: +6−2=+4 m. Total distance is 8 m, but displacement includes direction and endpoints.

questions.question: A car's speed increases from 5 m·s⁻¹ to 17 m·s⁻¹ in 4 s. Find its acceleration.
questions.explanation: a=(v−u)/Δt=(17−5)/4=3 m·s⁻². Divide the change in velocity, not the final velocity, by time.

questions.question: An object moves at constant velocity 8 m·s⁻¹ for 6 s. Find its displacement.
questions.explanation: At constant velocity, Δx=vΔt=8×6=48 m. Acceleration is zero but displacement need not be zero.

questions.question: Balance H₂ + O₂ → H₂O using the smallest whole-number coefficients.
questions.explanation: 2H₂+O₂→2H₂O has 4 hydrogen and 2 oxygen atoms on both sides. Change coefficients, not chemical subscripts.

questions.question: A trolley travels east at constant velocity. A learner concludes no forces act on it. Which evaluation is correct?
options: Every force must be zero because velocity is constant.
The net force must point east because it is moving east.
The net force is zero; individual balanced forces may still act.
Gravity disappears whenever horizontal speed is constant.
questions.explanation: Constant velocity implies zero acceleration and therefore zero resultant force. Weight and normal force, for example, can act and balance; zero resultant is not absence of forces.

title: Physical Sciences · Grade 10 · Term 4: Chemical quantities and mechanics revision · Set A
subject: Physical Sciences

questions.question: Using M(H₂O) = 18 g·mol⁻¹, how many moles are in 36 g of water?
questions.explanation: n=m/M = 36/18 = 2 mol. Molar mass links a measured mass to amount of substance.

questions.question: How many particles are in 0.5 mol? Use Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
questions.explanation: N=nNₐ = 0.5×6.02×10²³. Half a mole contains half Avogadro's number of particles.

questions.question: An object starts from rest with constant acceleration 2 m·s⁻² for 3 s. Find its displacement.
questions.explanation: Δx=uΔt+½aΔt²=0+½×2×3²=9 m. Include the square on time.

questions.question: A 2 kg object moves at 3 m·s⁻¹. Find its kinetic energy.
questions.explanation: Eₖ=½mv²=½×2×3²=9 J. Speed is squared, so kinetic energy is not simply mass times speed.

questions.question: Two identical balls move at speeds v and 2v. A learner claims the second has twice the kinetic energy. Which correction is justified?
options: It has the same energy because masses are equal.
It has half the energy because speed is greater.
It has four times the kinetic energy because energy depends on v².
It has eight times the energy because speed is cubed.
questions.explanation: For equal masses, Eₖ=½mv² gives an energy ratio (2v)²/v²=4. Comparing the proportional relationship reveals the error without needing a numerical mass.

title: Physical Sciences · Grade 11 · Term 2: Electricity and intermolecular forces · Set A
subject: Physical Sciences

questions.question: A 6 Ω resistor carries 2 A. Find the potential difference across it.
questions.explanation: Ohm's law gives V=IR=2×6=12 V for an ohmic resistor under constant physical conditions.

questions.question: A device operates at 12 V and 3 A. Find its electrical power.
questions.explanation: P=VI=12×3=36 W. Power is the rate of energy transfer, measured in watts.

questions.question: Which intermolecular force is especially important between water molecules?
options: Ionic bonding between whole water molecules
Covalent bonding between separate water molecules
questions.explanation: Water has H bonded to O and oxygen lone pairs, enabling hydrogen bonds between molecules. O–H covalent bonds are within each molecule.

questions.question: A coil experiences a larger rate of change of magnetic flux. What happens to the magnitude of induced emf, all else equal?
options: It depends only on the coil's colour
questions.explanation: Faraday's law relates induced emf magnitude to the rate of change of flux linkage. Faster change gives a larger emf for the same coil.

questions.question: A learner uses increasingly large currents to test Ohm's law in a metal wire without allowing it to cool. Which limitation matters most?
options: Current cannot be measured in a wire.
Potential difference is always independent of current.
Heating changes resistance, so physical conditions are not constant.
A wire's colour alone controls the result.
questions.explanation: Ohm's law requires constant physical conditions. Increased current can heat the wire and alter its resistance, confounding a comparison intended to test V proportional to I.

title: Physical Sciences · Grade 11 · Term 3: Stoichiometry, gases and energy change · Set A
subject: Physical Sciences

questions.question: A sample has mass 8 g and molar mass 16 g·mol⁻¹. Find its amount of substance.
questions.explanation: n=m/M=8/16=0.5 mol. Dividing by molar mass cancels grams and leaves moles.

questions.question: For 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, how many moles of O₂ react with 6 mol H₂, with enough O₂ available?
questions.explanation: The mole ratio H₂:O₂ is 2:1, so 6 mol H₂ needs 6/2=3 mol O₂. Coefficients describe mole ratios, not gram ratios.

questions.question: A fixed amount of gas occupies 4 L at 100 kPa. At constant temperature, find its volume at 200 kPa.
questions.explanation: Boyle's law: P₁V₁=P₂V₂. V₂=100×4/200=2 L. Doubling pressure halves volume at constant temperature.

questions.question: In an exothermic reaction, how does the enthalpy of products compare with reactants?
options: It is higher, so ΔH is positive
It is lower, so ΔH is negative
questions.explanation: Energy is released to surroundings. ΔH=H(products)−H(reactants) is negative because products have lower enthalpy.

questions.question: A sealed gas sample is compressed from 4 L to 2 L while warming. A learner uses Boyle's law to assert its pressure exactly doubles. What is missing?
options: The assertion is exact at every temperature.
The temperature change; Boyle's law alone requires constant temperature.
Compression means the number of molecules must halve.
questions.explanation: For a fixed amount of gas, PV/T is constant in the ideal model. Pressure also depends on absolute temperature; warming means the constant-temperature doubling claim is unjustified.

title: Physical Sciences · Grade 11 · Term 4: Acid–base and redox reactions · Set A
subject: Physical Sciences

questions.question: In the Brønsted–Lowry model, an acid is a…
questions.explanation: A Brønsted–Lowry acid donates H⁺. A base accepts H⁺, so identify the proton transfer in the reaction.

questions.question: For Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻, what happens to zinc?
options: It is reduced by losing electrons
It is oxidised by losing electrons
questions.explanation: Oxidation is loss of electrons. Zinc's oxidation number rises from 0 to +2.

questions.question: Which equation shows neutralisation of HCl by NaOH?
questions.explanation: The acid and base produce salt and water. Check that hydrogen and oxygen atoms are conserved as well as sodium and chlorine.

questions.question: A solution contains 0.2 mol solute in 0.5 dm³. Find its concentration.
questions.explanation: c=n/V=0.2/0.5=0.4 mol·dm⁻³. Use volume in dm³, not an unconverted millilitre value.

questions.question: A learner dilutes 100 mL of 0.4 mol·dm⁻³ solution to a final volume of 400 mL and claims the moles become one quarter. Which correction is right?
options: Moles become 0.01 mol; concentration stays 0.4 mol·dm⁻³.
Both moles and concentration remain unchanged.
Moles remain 0.04 mol; concentration becomes 0.1 mol·dm⁻³.
Adding water creates additional solute moles.
questions.explanation: Initial moles are 0.4×0.100=0.04 mol. Without loss or reaction, dilution changes volume, not solute amount. Final concentration is 0.04/0.400=0.1 mol·dm⁻³.

title: Physical Sciences · Grade 12 · Term 2: Work, Doppler effect and equilibrium · Set A
subject: Physical Sciences

questions.question: A constant 20 N force acts parallel to a 3 m displacement. Find the work done by this force.
questions.explanation: W=FΔx cosθ. Here θ=0°, so cosθ=1 and W=20×3=60 J. Only the parallel component does work.

questions.question: An ambulance approaches a stationary observer. Compared with the emitted sound, the observed frequency is…
questions.explanation: Approaching motion compresses the wavefront spacing at the observer, increasing observed frequency. This is the Doppler effect.

questions.question: For N₂(g)+3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), what does increasing pressure by reducing volume favour at constant temperature?
options: The reverse reaction, with fewer gas moles
Neither direction because gas amounts are equal
The forward reaction, with fewer gas moles
questions.explanation: There are 4 stoichiometric moles of gas on the left and 2 on the right. Compression favours the side with fewer gas moles.

questions.question: What does a catalyst change in a reaction at equilibrium?
options: The rates of both forward and reverse reactions, not the equilibrium constant at fixed temperature
The equilibrium constant at unchanged temperature
The final equilibrium composition by itself
questions.explanation: A catalyst offers a lower-activation-energy pathway for both directions. Equilibrium is reached faster without shifting its position at the same temperature.

questions.question: A catalyst is added to a sealed system already at equilibrium at constant temperature. A learner predicts a larger final product yield. Which evaluation is valid?
options: Only the forward reaction speeds up, increasing final yield.
The catalyst changes the equilibrium constant at this temperature.
The catalyst speeds both directions but does not change the equilibrium composition.
All reactions stop once the catalyst is added.
questions.explanation: A catalyst provides lower-activation-energy pathways in both directions. At fixed temperature it does not alter the equilibrium constant or equilibrium yield; it affects the approach to equilibrium.

title: Physical Sciences · Grade 12 · Term 3: Electric circuits, photoelectric effect and cells · Set A
subject: Physical Sciences

questions.question: A cell has emf 12 V and internal resistance 1 Ω. It supplies 2 A. Find its terminal potential difference.
questions.explanation: V=ε−Ir=12−2×1=10 V while supplying current. The internal resistor accounts for the lost volts.

questions.question: In a galvanic cell, oxidation occurs at the…
questions.explanation: Oxidation always occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode. In a galvanic cell, electrons flow externally from anode to cathode.

questions.question: Light below a metal's threshold frequency shines on it. Increasing intensity alone will…
options: Not cause photoemission in the standard single-photon model
Reduce the metal's work function to zero
questions.explanation: Each photon's energy is hf. Below threshold, individual photons lack enough energy to eject electrons; greater intensity does not raise their frequency.

questions.question: A generator converts predominantly which energy into electrical energy?
options: Nuclear energy directly with no process
questions.explanation: Relative motion in a magnetic field induces emf. Mechanical input drives the generator, transferring energy to the electrical circuit.

questions.question: A metal emits no electrons under light below its threshold frequency. Which experiment best distinguishes the photon model from an intensity-only explanation?
options: Change metal, frequency and intensity together with no record.
Count electrons once without measuring the light.
Keep frequency below threshold and increase intensity; then raise frequency above threshold.
Assume all bright light must eject electrons.
questions.explanation: Below threshold, extra intensity alone does not cause standard single-photon emission. Crossing the frequency threshold tests the photon-energy condition while staged changes avoid confounding variables.

title: Physical Sciences · Grade 12 · Term 4: Physics and chemistry examination revision · Set A
subject: Physical Sciences

questions.question: A 2 kg trolley changes velocity from 1 to 4 m·s⁻¹ east. Find the change in momentum.
questions.explanation: Δp=m(v−u)=2(4−1)=6 kg·m·s⁻¹ east. Final momentum alone is 8, not the change.

questions.question: Find the pH of a strong monoprotic acid with [H₃O⁺] = 1 × 10⁻³ mol·dm⁻³.
questions.explanation: pH=−log₁₀[H₃O⁺]=−log₁₀(10⁻³)=3. The minus sign reverses the exponent's sign.

questions.question: For an exothermic forward reaction, increasing temperature shifts equilibrium towards…
questions.explanation: Heat is effectively a product in an exothermic reaction. Increasing temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction, increasing the proportion of reactants.

questions.question: A metal has work function 3 eV; incident photons have energy 5 eV. Find the maximum photoelectron kinetic energy.
questions.explanation: Einstein's equation gives Kₘₐₓ=E(photon)−W₀=5−3=2 eV. Some photon energy frees the electron before any appears as kinetic energy.

questions.question: A trolley's momentum changes by 6 kg·m·s⁻¹. Two bumpers produce this same change in 0.1 s and 0.3 s. Which safety argument is justified?
options: The 0.3 s bumper gives three times the average net force.
Both average forces must be equal because impulse is equal.
The 0.3 s bumper gives one third of the average net force.
Longer stopping time must increase the momentum change.
questions.explanation: Average net force is impulse divided by contact time. The same 6 N·s gives 60 N over 0.1 s and 20 N over 0.3 s; longer time lowers the average force.

title: Life Sciences · Grade 10 · Term 2: Plant transport and animal circulation · Set A
subject: Life Sciences

questions.question: Which tissue transports most water and mineral salts from roots towards leaves?
questions.explanation: Xylem vessels provide a transport pathway for water and dissolved minerals. Phloem mainly transports organic nutrients such as sucrose.

questions.question: Why can closing stomata reduce water loss?
options: It stops all root absorption permanently
It reduces the pathway for water vapour to diffuse out
It increases the number of open pores
questions.explanation: Stomata are pores through which water vapour exits. Closing them reduces transpiration, although it can also limit carbon dioxide entry.

questions.question: Which blood vessel carries blood away from the heart?
questions.explanation: Arteries carry blood away from the heart. Direction defines the vessel; not all arteries carry oxygenated blood.

questions.question: Why is a red blood cell's biconcave shape useful?
options: It makes the cell a rigid cube
It gives a large surface area relative to volume for gas exchange
questions.explanation: The shape supports rapid gas exchange over a short diffusion distance. Haemoglobin within the cell binds oxygen.

questions.question: A class coats the lower leaf surfaces of one plant with petroleum jelly and leaves a similar plant uncoated. Both lose mass. Which finding would support reduced transpiration due to coating?
options: The coated plant is kept cooler and watered less than the control.
Only the uncoated plant's starting mass is recorded.
The coated plant loses less mass, with soil evaporation controlled in both.
Any mass loss proves the coating has no effect.
questions.explanation: Compare changes under otherwise similar conditions and cover the soil to limit evaporation. Less mass loss then supports reduced leaf water loss; it need not eliminate all water loss.

title: Life Sciences · Grade 10 · Term 3: Ecosystems, fossils and classification · Set A
subject: Life Sciences

questions.question: In grass → grasshopper → frog, what is the grasshopper?
questions.explanation: Grass is the producer. The grasshopper eats the producer, so it is the primary consumer; the frog is a secondary consumer.

questions.question: Which is an abiotic factor in a pond?
questions.explanation: Abiotic factors are non-living physical or chemical conditions. Living organisms are biotic factors.

questions.question: Why are fossils useful when studying life's history?
options: They prove every past organism was preserved
They show all species existed at the same time
They cannot be compared with living organisms
They provide evidence of organisms and environments from the past
questions.explanation: The fossil record documents past life and changes through time, but preservation is incomplete and biased towards suitable conditions.

questions.question: Which scientific name is correctly written in plain text?
questions.explanation: The genus begins with a capital and the species epithet with lowercase. In formatted writing both are italicised, or separately underlined when handwritten.

questions.question: Frogs decline after a pesticide is introduced near a pond. Which evidence best tests whether the pesticide contributed?
options: A photograph of one frog before spraying.
The assumption that every population change has a single cause.
Repeated frog counts and exposure measurements at treated and comparable untreated ponds.
Counts only at the treated pond on one day.
questions.explanation: Comparison sites and repeated exposure and population measurements help separate pesticide effects from weather, habitat change and natural variation. Timing alone is insufficient causal evidence.

title: Life Sciences · Grade 10 · Term 4: Biodiversity and year-end consolidation · Set A
subject: Life Sciences

questions.question: Which group has cells without a membrane-bound nucleus?
questions.explanation: Bacteria are prokaryotes. Their DNA is not enclosed in a membrane-bound nucleus, unlike the eukaryotic groups listed.

questions.question: Why are fungi not classified as plants?
options: They obtain organic nutrients rather than photosynthesising like green plants
questions.explanation: Fungi are heterotrophs and absorb nutrients. Their cell walls typically contain chitin, rather than the cellulose characteristic of plants.

questions.question: Which feature is shared by plants and animals?
options: They both have chloroplasts in every cell
They both have cellulose cell walls
questions.explanation: Plants and animals are eukaryotes with membrane-bound nuclei. Animal cells do not have chloroplasts or cellulose walls.

questions.question: A learner says all microorganisms are harmful. Which correction is best?
options: Many microorganisms are beneficial, including decomposers
questions.explanation: Many microbes break down organic matter and recycle nutrients; others are useful in food production. Some cause disease, but the claim generalises incorrectly.

questions.question: A culture of microorganisms grows on dead plant material. A learner calls all of them harmful. Which evaluation is best?
options: Growth on dead material proves every organism causes human disease.
Anything too small to see has no ecological role.
Decomposition may recycle nutrients; identify organisms and effects before classifying harm.
Microorganisms are always beneficial and never pathogenic.
questions.explanation: Microorganisms have diverse roles, including decomposition and disease. The observed nutrient-recycling activity does not support an unrestricted claim that all are harmful.

title: Life Sciences · Grade 11 · Term 2: Photosynthesis, respiration and nutrition · Set A
subject: Life Sciences

questions.question: Which gas is taken in as a raw material for photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water to produce organic compounds using light energy. Oxygen is released as a by-product.

questions.question: Why does increasing light eventually stop increasing photosynthesis rate in a healthy plant?
options: Another factor, such as CO₂ or temperature, becomes limiting
The plant stops needing glucose permanently
questions.explanation: Once light is no longer limiting, another required factor limits the rate. Experiments should keep other conditions controlled.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of cellular respiration?
options: To transfer energy from organic molecules into ATP
To remove every oxygen atom from the body
questions.explanation: Respiration releases energy through reactions and captures some in ATP, which powers cellular processes. It is not the same as breathing.

questions.question: Where does most absorption of digested nutrients occur in humans?
questions.explanation: The small intestine has villi and microvilli that increase surface area for absorption of digested nutrients.

questions.question: A plant produces 10 bubbles per minute at low light and 10 at high light. Which next test best investigates a possible limiting factor?
options: Change light, CO₂ and temperature together without controls.
Conclude light never affects photosynthesis in any plant.
Increase available CO₂ at high light while controlling temperature and other conditions.
Count bubbles once and call it conclusive.
questions.explanation: A plateau may reflect a different limiting factor. Changing CO₂ while holding other conditions constant tests that explanation; repeat measurements because bubble counts are only an approximate rate indicator.

title: Life Sciences · Grade 11 · Term 3: Gas exchange, excretion and populations · Set A
subject: Life Sciences

questions.question: Why are alveolar walls thin and moist?
options: To support rapid diffusion of gases
questions.explanation: A thin surface shortens diffusion distance; moisture allows gases to dissolve before diffusing across the exchange surface.

questions.question: Which organ removes urea from the blood and helps regulate water balance?
questions.explanation: Kidneys filter blood and form urine, removing nitrogenous wastes and regulating water and salts. The liver produces urea from excess amino nitrogen.

questions.question: What happens when ADH secretion increases in a healthy person?
options: Less water is reabsorbed and all urine stops
More water is reabsorbed, usually producing a smaller volume of more concentrated urine
questions.explanation: ADH increases water reabsorption in the kidney, generally reducing urine volume and making it more concentrated. Distinguish urine volume from concentration.

questions.question: A population gains 30 births and 10 immigrants, with 20 deaths and 5 emigrants. Find its net change.
questions.explanation: Change = births+immigration−deaths−emigration = 30+10−20−5 = +15 individuals.

questions.question: A population rises by 15 after 30 births, 20 deaths, 10 immigrants and 5 emigrants. Which prediction about next year is warranted?
options: It must rise by exactly 15 every year.
Births alone guarantee a rise of 30.
No exact prediction follows without next year's rates and conditions.
questions.explanation: The net change describes one interval: 30+10−20−5=15. Future births, deaths, migration and resource limits may differ, so extrapolating the same change as a certainty is unjustified.

title: Life Sciences · Grade 11 · Term 4: Human impact and environmental evidence · Set A
subject: Life Sciences

questions.question: How can excess fertiliser entering a dam harm aquatic life?
options: It permanently increases oxygen in all depths
It can cause algal growth and oxygen depletion during decomposition
It stops all biological activity immediately
It turns fresh water directly into salt water
questions.explanation: Nutrient enrichment can cause eutrophication. Decomposers use dissolved oxygen as excess organic material breaks down, threatening aquatic organisms.

questions.question: Why does destroying wetlands threaten water quality?
options: Wetlands have no role in water movement
Wetlands can trap sediments and help filter pollutants
Wetlands prevent every flood regardless of size
questions.explanation: Wetlands provide important filtration and flow-regulation services. Their protection reduces risks, although it cannot eliminate all pollution or flooding.

questions.question: Which action most directly lowers a school's electricity-related carbon footprint when electricity comes from fossil fuels?
options: Replace every indigenous tree with concrete
questions.explanation: Using less fossil-fuel-generated electricity reduces associated emissions. Measure energy use to assess whether the intervention works.

questions.question: A study links habitat fragmentation to falling species numbers. What strengthens its conclusion?
options: Compare repeated data from fragmented and less-fragmented sites while considering other causes
Assume correlation proves the only cause
questions.explanation: Repeated comparable observations and consideration of confounding factors support stronger evidence. A single correlation is not proof of sole causation.

questions.question: A dam has an algal bloom followed by fish deaths. Which evidence most directly tests oxygen depletion during decomposition?
options: Only the colour of a poster about the dam.
A count of fish species with no water measurements.
Dissolved-oxygen measurements over time, compared with less-affected water and decomposition indicators.
An assumption that all algae directly poison every fish.
questions.explanation: Tracking oxygen decline alongside organic decay tests the proposed mechanism. Comparison water and repeated measurements help distinguish it from other causes such as a toxic discharge.

title: Life Sciences · Grade 12 · Term 2: Inheritance and human responses · Set A
subject: Life Sciences

questions.question: In a monohybrid cross Aa × Aa with complete dominance, P(aa) is…
questions.explanation: The four equally likely combinations are AA, Aa, Aa and aa. Only one is homozygous recessive.

questions.question: What connects a sensory receptor to the central nervous system in a simple reflex pathway?
questions.explanation: A sensory neuron carries impulses from a receptor towards the CNS. A motor neuron carries impulses from the CNS to an effector.

questions.question: Why is insulin release after a meal an example of negative feedback?
options: It helps bring raised blood glucose back towards its normal range
It keeps increasing blood glucose without limit
It prevents glucose uptake by all cells
questions.explanation: Raised blood glucose stimulates insulin release. Its effects reduce blood glucose, opposing the original change.

questions.question: A shoot bends towards light. What is this response called?
questions.explanation: Phototropism is growth in response to directional light. Growth towards the stimulus is positive; differential growth causes the bending.

questions.question: Two parents with a dominant phenotype have a child with a recessive phenotype for a simple complete-dominance trait. What follows, assuming the model applies?
options: One recessive child means all later children must be recessive.
Neither parent can carry a recessive allele.
Both parents must carry the recessive allele, but the next child's phenotype is not fixed.
The next child must be dominant to balance the ratio.
questions.explanation: A recessive child is aa, requiring an a allele from each parent. Dominant parents must therefore both be Aa; each new conception has its own 1/4 probability of aa.

title: Life Sciences · Grade 12 · Term 3: Evolution and interpreting evidence · Set A
subject: Life Sciences

questions.question: A population has inherited variation in beak size. A food change favours larger beaks. What explains larger beaks becoming more common over generations?
options: Every bird consciously enlarges its beak
The environment directly rewrites every bird's genes in the same way
Individuals evolve because they need to survive
Individuals with advantageous inherited traits leave more surviving offspring
questions.explanation: Natural selection acts on existing heritable variation. Changes in reproductive success alter trait frequencies across generations, not by individual intention.

questions.question: What is required for populations to become separate species through reproductive isolation?
options: They cease exchanging genes and diverge sufficiently
They must become identical in every feature
They must live on different planets
questions.explanation: Restricted gene flow allows divergence. Speciation involves reproductive isolation, not simply living far apart for a short time.

questions.question: How do homologous structures support common ancestry?
options: They share an underlying structural pattern despite possible differences in function
They prove organisms are the same species
They arise only from identical environments
questions.explanation: Shared underlying structure is consistent with descent from a common ancestor, modified for different uses. Similar function alone can instead reflect analogy.

questions.question: Which finding supports an African origin of modern humans?
options: The claim that living humans belong to separate biological races ranked by ability
The claim that evolution stopped outside Africa
Fossil and genetic evidence consistent with early modern humans in Africa and later dispersal
The absence of all fossils outside Africa
questions.explanation: The Out-of-Africa model is supported by multiple lines of fossil and genetic evidence. It does not rank living populations or deny later migration and interbreeding.

questions.question: After drought, large-beaked birds become more common. Which additional evidence best supports natural selection rather than a temporary change within individuals?
options: Each bird reports trying harder to grow a beak.
Only the population's location is recorded.
Beak-size variation is inherited and larger-beaked birds leave more surviving offspring.
A single adult changes its posture for a photograph.
questions.explanation: Natural selection requires heritable variation and differential reproductive success. A change in frequency alone needs evidence linking the trait to inheritance and survival or reproduction.

title: Life Sciences · Grade 12 · Term 4: Integrated biological reasoning revision · Set A
subject: Life Sciences

questions.question: DNA has 20% adenine in a double-stranded molecule. Approximately what percentage is guanine?
questions.explanation: A pairs with T, so T is 20%. The remaining 60% is G+C, split equally: G=30%.

questions.question: Why does meiosis contribute to variation?
options: It produces only genetically identical gametes
Crossing over and independent assortment produce different allele combinations
It doubles chromosome number in each gamete
questions.explanation: Crossing over and independent chromosome assortment create different combinations. Meiosis also halves chromosome number for sexual reproduction.

questions.question: A healthy person becomes dehydrated. Which response helps conserve water?
options: Decreased ADH and unlimited water loss
Kidneys stop responding to hormones permanently
Increased ADH and increased kidney water reabsorption
More dilute urine in every circumstance
questions.explanation: Dehydration generally stimulates ADH release, promoting water reabsorption and smaller volumes of concentrated urine.

questions.question: A farmer claims pesticide resistance appears because insects try harder to survive. Which correction is best?
options: All insects choose new genes on exposure
Pesticide makes every insect equally resistant immediately
Inherited resistant variants survive and reproduce more successfully under pesticide selection
questions.explanation: Selection favours existing resistant variants or variants arising through mutation. Their descendants become more common; effort does not direct genetic change.

questions.question: A pesticide kills 95% of insects. Survivors produce offspring that also resist it. What control-study evidence would strengthen an inherited-resistance explanation?
options: Every survivor is assumed to have chosen resistance.
Only the pesticide bottle's colour is recorded.
Resistance persists in offspring raised without pesticide and differs from a susceptible comparison line.
No offspring are tested because survival proves inheritance.
questions.explanation: Raising offspring without exposure helps distinguish inherited resistance from an immediate environmental response. A susceptible comparison and repeated trials strengthen the interpretation.

title: Accounting · Grade 10 · Term 2: Journals, payroll and adjustments · Set A
subject: Accounting

questions.question: A business buys trading stock on credit. Which journal usually records this purchase?
questions.explanation: A credit purchase of stock from a supplier belongs in the creditors journal. No cash moves at purchase, so a cash journal is inappropriate.

questions.question: Gross pay is R6 000 and employee deductions total R800. Find net pay.
questions.explanation: Net pay = gross pay−employee deductions = R5 200. Employer contributions are a separate concept.

questions.question: Why compare the debtors control balance with the debtors list total?
options: To guarantee all customers have paid
To identify differences that need investigation
questions.explanation: The control account should reconcile with the total individual debtors' balances. Differences may indicate errors requiring correction.

questions.question: Equipment costing R20 000 depreciates at 10% per year on cost. Find one full year's depreciation.
questions.explanation: Depreciation = cost×rate×time = 20 000×0.10×1 = R2 000. R18 000 is the carrying value after this charge.

questions.question: The debtors control balance exceeds the debtors list by R500. A clerk proposes writing off R500 immediately. Which response is best?
options: Write off R500 solely to force the totals to agree.
Increase sales by R500 without a source document.
Trace entries and reconcile the difference before making a supported correction.
Ignore the difference because control accounts cannot be wrong.
questions.explanation: A difference signals an error or omission, not its cause. Check journals, postings and source documents, then correct the identified error with an audit trail rather than inventing a balancing entry.

title: Accounting · Grade 10 · Term 3: Financial statements and indicators · Set A
subject: Accounting

questions.question: Sales are R80 000 and cost of sales R50 000. Find gross profit.
questions.explanation: Gross profit = sales−cost of sales = R30 000. Operating expenses are deducted later when calculating net profit.

questions.question: Gross profit is R30 000 and sales R80 000. Find gross profit as a percentage of sales.
questions.explanation: 30 000/80 000×100 = 37.5%. A percentage of cost of sales would have a different denominator.

questions.question: Rent of R1 000 is owed for the current year but unpaid at year end. What adjustment is needed?
options: Increase rent expense and recognise an accrued-expense liability
Decrease rent expense and create an asset
questions.explanation: Accrual accounting records the expense in the period incurred. The unpaid amount creates a liability.

questions.question: Current assets total R60 000 and current liabilities R30 000. Find the current ratio.
questions.explanation: Current ratio = current assets/current liabilities = 60 000/30 000 = 2:1. It is one indicator of short-term liquidity, not a guarantee of solvency.

questions.question: A business has current assets R60 000, including R45 000 slow-moving stock, and current liabilities R30 000. Why is its 2:1 current ratio insufficient reassurance?
options: A 2:1 ratio guarantees every debt can be paid immediately.
Stock is always equivalent to cash on demand.
Only R15 000 of current assets excludes stock, so near-term cash needs require further investigation.
Current liabilities must be zero whenever current assets are larger.
questions.explanation: The current ratio includes inventory, which may not sell promptly. Excluding stock gives 15 000/30 000=0.5:1; investigate collections, stock movement and payment timing before judging liquidity.

title: Accounting · Grade 10 · Term 4: Manufacturing costs and budgets · Set A
subject: Accounting

questions.question: Which cost is usually direct material for a furniture manufacturer?
questions.explanation: Direct materials can be traced to the product. Timber becomes part of each chair; administration and advertising are not direct materials.

questions.question: Direct materials cost R8 000 and direct labour R5 000. Find prime cost.
questions.explanation: Prime cost = direct materials + direct labour = R13 000. Factory overheads are added separately for total production cost.

questions.question: A cash budget opens with R4 000, receives R9 000 and pays R10 000. Find its closing balance.
questions.explanation: Closing cash = opening cash+receipts−payments = 4 000+9 000−10 000 = R3 000. Opening cash must be included.

questions.question: Which item is excluded from cash payments in a cash budget?
questions.explanation: Depreciation is a non-cash expense. Equipment purchased for cash is a cash payment even though it is a capital item.

questions.question: A cash budget shows a R3 000 closing balance after excluding depreciation of R1 000. A learner deducts depreciation again. Which judgement is correct?
options: Reduce cash to R2 000 because every expense is a payment.
Increase cash to R4 000 because depreciation creates cash.
Keep R3 000; depreciation is not a cash payment in this budget.
Treat depreciation as a receipt from customers.
questions.explanation: Depreciation allocates an asset's cost as an expense without a current cash outflow. Deducting it in a cash budget would understate cash; actual asset purchases are considered separately.

title: Accounting · Grade 11 · Term 2: Partnership statements and analysis · Set A
subject: Accounting

questions.question: A partnership earns R90 000 before appropriations. Partner salaries total R30 000; no other appropriations apply. Find residual profit.
questions.explanation: Residual profit = profit available−partner salaries−other appropriations. Here 90 000−30 000=R60 000, shared using the agreed ratio.

questions.question: Residual profit of R60 000 is shared A:B = 2:1. What is B's share?
questions.explanation: The ratio has three parts. B receives one part: 60 000/3 = R20 000. Do not divide by B's ratio number alone.

questions.question: A business has current assets R120 000 including stock R40 000, and current liabilities R50 000. Find the acid-test ratio.
questions.explanation: Acid-test ratio = (current assets−inventory)/current liabilities = (120 000−40 000)/50 000 = 1.6:1.

questions.question: Why compare a partnership's financial indicators with prior years?
options: To prove future profit is guaranteed
To avoid reading the financial statements
To identify trends and investigate performance changes
questions.explanation: Comparisons help interpret performance, but context such as changing prices, policies and business conditions still matters.

questions.question: A partnership's profit rises but its acid-test ratio falls from 1.6:1 to 0.7:1. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Higher profit proves all short-term debts are affordable.
A falling acid-test ratio proves theft occurred.
Profitability improved, but short-term liquidity needs separate investigation.
Profit and cash availability are always identical.
questions.explanation: Profit is measured on an accrual basis, while the acid-test ratio compares more liquid assets with current liabilities. Examine cash flows, debtor collections and payment dates before deciding on action.

title: Accounting · Grade 11 · Term 3: Budgets, inventory and manufacturing · Set A
subject: Accounting

questions.question: A cash sale of R500 occurs in March. Where does it appear in the cash budget?
options: Nowhere because sales are not cash
questions.explanation: A cash budget records the timing of actual cash movements. A cash sale is received in March; credit collections need a collection schedule.

questions.question: A business expects 60% of credit sales of R20 000 to be collected next month. Find that collection.
questions.explanation: Multiply credit sales by the collection proportion: 20 000×0.60=R12 000. The rest is collected later or subject to other assumptions.

questions.question: Fixed costs are R30 000; selling price is R50 per unit and variable cost R20. Find break-even units.
questions.explanation: Contribution per unit = 50−20=R30. Break-even = fixed costs/contribution = 30 000/30 = 1 000 units.

questions.question: Which statement distinguishes perpetual from periodic inventory?
options: Perpetual records continuously update stock and cost of sales; periodic calculates cost of sales at intervals
Periodic means stock is never counted
Perpetual means stock cannot be stolen
questions.explanation: The systems differ in recording timing. Physical stocktaking remains useful for verifying balances and identifying losses.

questions.question: A business forecasts R12 000 collections next month from R20 000 credit sales. Debtor payment delays are increasing. What is the best budget response?
options: Keep the forecast unchanged because a policy guarantees payment.
Record all R20 000 as cash received immediately.
Test lower or later collections and plan for possible funding needs.
Remove all sales from the income statement.
questions.explanation: A collection policy is an estimate, not a guarantee. Actual debtor behaviour informs a more realistic timing forecast; sensitivity checks show the cash effect of delayed or reduced receipts.

title: Accounting · Grade 11 · Term 4: VAT and accounting revision · Set A
subject: Accounting

questions.question: For this exercise VAT is 15%. A cash sale of R1 000 excluding VAT creates output VAT of…
questions.explanation: Output VAT is charged on taxable sales: 1 000×0.15=R150. The VAT-inclusive receipt is R1 150.

questions.question: Output VAT is R9 000 and deductible input VAT R6 500. Find the net VAT payable.
questions.explanation: Net VAT payable = output−deductible input = R2 500. If deductible input exceeded output, the position would instead be receivable, subject to rules.

questions.question: For this exercise VAT is 15%. Extract VAT from a VAT-inclusive amount of R230.
questions.explanation: VAT = inclusive amount×15/115 = 230×15/115 = R30. Taking 15% of the inclusive total uses the wrong base.

questions.question: Why keep a valid tax invoice for a purchase?
options: It guarantees every expense is deductible
It supports the accounting record and any qualifying input-VAT claim
It replaces the need to pay the supplier
It allows any invented VAT claim
questions.explanation: Reliable documentation supports verification. Input VAT is subject to qualifying rules, so an invoice alone does not make every purchase claimable.

questions.question: A VAT return includes an input claim supported only by a handwritten total with no valid tax invoice. What should the accountant do?
options: Claim it automatically because any total proves eligibility.
Create an invoice in the supplier's name without authorisation.
Verify eligibility and obtain the required evidence before including the claim.
Increase output VAT to hide the unsupported claim.
questions.explanation: An input-VAT claim needs qualifying expenditure and supporting documentation under applicable rules. Investigate and obtain valid evidence rather than fabricate records or assume every purchase qualifies.

subject: Accounting

questions.question: A FIFO system has 10 units at R20, followed by 10 at R30. Twelve units are sold. Find cost of sales.
questions.explanation: FIFO issues the oldest units first: 10×20 + 2×30 = R260. The remaining eight units are from the R30 batch.

questions.question: Fixed costs are R120 000 and contribution is R40 per unit. Find break-even units.
questions.explanation: Break-even units = fixed costs/contribution per unit = 120 000/40 = 3 000. Contribution is selling price less variable cost.

questions.question: An asset costs R100 000; accumulated depreciation is R35 000. Find its carrying value.
questions.explanation: Carrying value = cost−accumulated depreciation = R65 000. It need not equal the asset's market value.

questions.question: Why separate asset custody from record keeping where practical?
options: To reduce the risk of undetected error or fraud
To make records confidential from auditors
questions.explanation: Segregation of duties makes unauthorised actions harder to conceal. It reduces risk but requires checks and does not eliminate every risk.

questions.question: Two inventory methods give different profits during rising purchase prices, with identical sales and physical stock. What should an analyst check first?
options: Which method changes the actual number of units sold.
Whether a higher accounting profit guarantees more cash.
The valuation method and its effect on cost of sales and closing inventory.
Whether stock costing can replace a physical count.
questions.explanation: Different cost-flow assumptions can allocate different purchase costs to sales and closing inventory. Understand the method before comparing profits; it does not itself change physical units or cash already paid.

title: Accounting · Grade 12 · Term 3: VAT and forward-looking budgets · Set A
subject: Accounting

questions.question: For this exercise output VAT is R18 000 and deductible input VAT R11 000. What is payable?
questions.explanation: Net VAT payable = output−deductible input = 18 000−11 000 = R7 000, assuming no other adjustments.

questions.question: Why does depreciation appear in a projected income statement but not as a cash-budget payment?
options: It is an expense without a current cash outflow
It is illegal in all budgets
It is paid to the bank every month
questions.explanation: The income statement forecasts profit using accrual expenses; a cash budget forecasts cash movements. Depreciation reduces profit without a cash payment in that period.

questions.question: Credit sales are R50 000. The collection policy expects 80% next month, with no discount. Find next month's receipt from these sales.
questions.explanation: Expected cash collection = 50 000×0.80 = R40 000. Record receipts in the month collected, not automatically when sold.

questions.question: A budget forecast shows a cash shortfall next month. Which response is most useful?
options: Ignore it until every supplier is overdue
Treat the forecast as a guaranteed bank balance
Investigate timing, reduce avoidable payments and plan funding early
questions.explanation: A cash forecast is an early warning. Review assumptions and practical actions; fabricating receipts hides rather than solves the problem.

questions.question: A profitable business forecasts a cash deficit because customers pay after supplier debts fall due. Which recommendation addresses the cause?
options: Increase depreciation to generate immediate cash.
Ignore the deficit because profit guarantees positive bank funds.
Negotiate payment timing and improve collections while assessing suitable short-term funding.
Record unpaid customer invoices as cash already received.
questions.explanation: The problem is the timing gap between receipts and payments. A cash forecast, collection action and negotiated terms address it; accrual profit and non-cash adjustments cannot guarantee immediate liquidity.

title: Accounting · Grade 12 · Term 4: Integrated financial and control revision · Set A
subject: Accounting

questions.question: Net profit after tax is R240 000 and average shareholders' equity R1 200 000. Find the return on average equity.
questions.explanation: Return = profit after tax/average equity×100 = 240 000/1 200 000×100=20%. Use the average equity specified.

questions.question: A company has current assets R300 000 and liabilities due within a year R200 000. Find the current ratio.
questions.explanation: Current ratio = current assets/current liabilities = 300 000/200 000=1.5:1. Assess stock quality and collection timing as well.

questions.question: Why should a bank reconciliation investigate unexplained differences?
options: All differences are automatically bank fraud
Reconciliation changes the bank's actual cash without evidence
A bank statement never contains errors
They may reveal recording errors, timing differences or unauthorised transactions
questions.explanation: Reconciliation compares independent records. Identify and substantiate each difference before recording any necessary correction.

questions.question: A company repays R40 000 of a loan using bank funds. What happens to total assets and liabilities?
questions.explanation: Bank, an asset, decreases and the loan liability decreases by the same amount. Repaying principal is not itself an expense.

questions.question: A business repays a R40 000 loan and its current ratio worsens. A director calls the repayment an expense that reduced profit. Which evaluation is sound?
options: Principal repayment always reduces profit by R40 000.
Loan principal reduces cash and liabilities; assess liquidity separately from interest expense.
A lower current ratio necessarily proves fraud.
questions.explanation: Repayment of principal reduces an asset and a liability, rather than being an operating expense. Interest is accounted for separately; the remaining cash and liability classification affect liquidity analysis.

title: Business Studies · Grade 10 · Term 2: Business sectors and ownership · Set A
subject: Business Studies

questions.question: A bakery turns flour into bread. Which economic sector describes this production?
questions.explanation: The secondary sector transforms raw materials into products. Farming wheat is primary; selling services is tertiary.

questions.question: Which feature usually distinguishes a sole proprietor?
options: Separate legal personality with shareholders by definition
One owner with unlimited personal liability
questions.explanation: A sole proprietor owns the business personally and generally bears its debts. This is a risk to consider alongside control and simplicity.

questions.question: A business supports a local reading programme. Which concept best fits?
questions.explanation: Supporting community well-being can be part of corporate social responsibility. Assess its real benefits rather than assuming every donation solves the issue.

questions.question: Why can unemployment affect a local shop's sales?
options: It guarantees higher sales for every shop
Lower household income can reduce demand
It changes a shop into a primary-sector business
questions.explanation: Unemployment can reduce customers' spending power. Businesses should examine local evidence and demand patterns rather than assume identical effects everywhere.

questions.question: A sole trader wants expansion finance but worries about personal exposure to business debts. Which decision process is strongest?
options: Choose solely by the most attractive business name.
Assume every ownership form gives identical personal liability.
Compare ownership forms, liability, control and costs before choosing.
Expand without reviewing finance or risk.
questions.explanation: Ownership choices involve trade-offs between liability, capital access, control and administration. A reasoned recommendation uses the owner's needs and the applicable legal features rather than a single superficial preference.

title: Business Studies · Grade 10 · Term 3: Problem solving, research and business plans · Set A
subject: Business Studies

questions.question: Customers complain about long queues. What should the business do first in a structured problem-solving process?
options: Copy a random competitor without analysis
Define and investigate the queue problem
questions.explanation: A clear problem definition and evidence help identify causes. Solutions should address the cause rather than a guessed symptom.

questions.question: Which example is primary market research?
options: Reading last year's published industry report
Using an old public census table
questions.explanation: Primary research collects new data for the current purpose. Published existing information is secondary research.

questions.question: Why include a cash-flow forecast in a business plan?
options: To guarantee every sale is cash
To anticipate when cash may be received and paid
To replace a description of customers
To prove the business cannot fail
questions.explanation: Timing matters: a profitable business can still run short of cash. A forecast supports planning, not certainty.

questions.question: Which slide design best supports a short business presentation?
options: A dense page of tiny text
A readable chart with a clear label and explained message
Animated text that hides the main point
questions.explanation: Visuals should make evidence easier to interpret. Explain units, meaning and source rather than expecting decoration to communicate the argument.

questions.question: A shop surveys only customers who bought immediately about long queues. Why might its proposed solution be weak?
options: Purchasers necessarily represent everyone who left.
A larger logo would remove sampling bias.
It excludes people who left without buying, whose experiences may reveal the main problem.
questions.explanation: The sample omits affected non-buyers and may underestimate queue-related lost sales. Include these customers where feasible and compare observations of waiting times before selecting a remedy.
