title: Business Studies · Grade 10 · Term 4: Relationships and team performance · Set A
subject: Business Studies

questions.question: A team has clear roles but members never share progress. What improvement is most useful?
options: Agree regular check-ins and shared communication
Stop all communication to avoid disagreement
Let every member assume others finished
questions.explanation: Clear communication helps coordinate interdependent tasks and identify problems early. Roles alone do not ensure collaboration.

questions.question: A manager allocates tasks using stereotypes about gender. Why is this harmful?
options: It is always the most accurate skills test
It can unfairly exclude capable people and damage trust
questions.explanation: Fair task allocation should consider skills and development needs. Stereotyping undermines inclusion and team performance.

questions.question: Which action best handles a disagreement about a deadline?
options: Listen to both views and agree a practical plan tied to the goal
questions.explanation: Constructive conflict management focuses on the issue, evidence and achievable agreements, with follow-up responsibilities.

questions.question: How can a team assess performance meaningfully?
options: Count only how often members smiled
Compare agreed objectives with results and discuss improvements
questions.explanation: Performance assessment needs relevant criteria and evidence. Reflect on process and outcomes to guide the next task.

questions.question: A team meets its deadline but one member did nearly all the work. Which evaluation best supports improvement?
options: A met deadline proves teamwork was effective in every respect.
Punish every member identically without hearing them.
Review both the output and the fairness of roles, communication and contribution.
Remove all role allocation from the next project.
questions.explanation: Performance includes process as well as output. Evidence about contributions and barriers helps redistribute tasks fairly and improve communication while recognising the completed result.

title: Business Studies · Grade 11 · Term 2: Marketing, production and ethical decisions · Set A
subject: Business Studies

questions.question: A business asks experts for anonymous opinions over several rounds. Which technique is this?
questions.explanation: Delphi collects expert judgments, shares summaries and repeats rounds. Anonymity can reduce the influence of dominant individuals.

questions.question: Which decision belongs to distribution policy?
options: What colour the logo should be only
How much tax a worker owes
Whether to sell directly or through retailers
questions.explanation: Distribution policy concerns how products reach customers. Channels can be direct or involve intermediaries.

questions.question: How does quality control differ from production planning?
options: Quality control guarantees zero defects forever
It checks outputs against standards; planning arranges production activities
questions.explanation: Production planning sets resources, sequence and timing. Quality control checks whether products meet defined standards.

questions.question: A salesperson knows a product has a defect but hides it. What is the ethical response?
options: Disclose relevant facts and follow the remedy process
Conceal the defect to secure the sale
Alter the receipt to hide evidence
questions.explanation: Honest disclosure and appropriate remedies support trust and ethical conduct. Professional behaviour does not mean maximising sales at any cost.

questions.question: A factory reduces inspection to cut costs, after which defects and returns rise. What should management evaluate?
options: Only the saving on inspection wages.
Only the number of adverts published.
Total quality costs, including prevention, inspection, returns and lost customers.
Whether customers can be prevented from reporting defects.
questions.explanation: An isolated cost reduction can increase total costs. Compare prevention and appraisal spending with internal and external failure costs, using evidence to choose a sustainable quality approach.

title: Business Studies · Grade 11 · Term 3: Action plans, presentations and team development · Set A
subject: Business Studies

questions.question: What does a Gantt chart show in an action plan?
options: Tasks and their timing along a timeline
questions.explanation: A Gantt chart shows when tasks start and finish, helping track overlapping work and dependencies.

questions.question: An entrepreneur tests a small version of a product before expanding. What does this demonstrate?
options: A guarantee that failure is impossible
questions.explanation: Testing assumptions can reduce uncertainty and reveal improvements. Entrepreneurial risk-taking can be informed and measured rather than reckless.

questions.question: During the storming stage, team members disagree about roles. What should a leader encourage?
options: Constructive discussion and clarification of expectations
questions.explanation: Storming may involve conflict as members establish roles. Clarifying norms and responsibilities helps the team move towards more effective collaboration.

questions.question: A presenter cannot answer a question confidently. What is the most professional response?
options: Acknowledge the gap and offer to verify and follow up
Pretend the question was never asked
questions.explanation: Honesty protects credibility. Clarify the question and commit to checking reliable information rather than fabricating an answer.

questions.question: A pilot product succeeds with ten loyal customers. Which expansion recommendation is most defensible?
options: Launch nationally because ten loyal users prove universal demand.
Cancel the product because small pilots never help.
Test demand in a broader target-market sample and update the action plan before scaling.
Copy the pilot result into every future forecast unchanged.
questions.explanation: A pilot provides useful but limited evidence. A broader relevant sample, cost estimates and milestones help judge whether the result will transfer to the intended market.

title: Business Studies · Grade 11 · Term 4: Recruitment, selection and induction · Set A
subject: Business Studies

questions.question: What is the main purpose of recruitment?
options: Choose a candidate before defining the job
Attract suitable applicants for a vacancy
questions.explanation: Recruitment creates a suitable applicant pool. Selection then evaluates applicants against job-related criteria.

questions.question: Which interview question is most appropriate for assessing a delivery planner?
options: Describe how you would prioritise delayed deliveries
Which unrelated political party does your family support?
Why should we ignore your skills?
Will you accept unsafe work without questions?
questions.explanation: Job-relevant questions provide evidence of competence. Irrelevant or discriminatory questions do not fairly assess ability.

questions.question: Why provide induction for a new employee?
options: Explain the role, workplace procedures and safety expectations
Guarantee the employee never needs support
questions.explanation: Induction helps employees understand duties, colleagues, policies and safety. It is a starting point for ongoing support.

questions.question: A worker earns R50 per hour for 20 hours. Before deductions, what is the pay?
questions.explanation: Time-related pay = hourly rate×hours = 50×20=R1 000. This is gross pay before any deductions.

questions.question: Two applicants have similar qualifications. An interviewer favours a friend without using job criteria. What is the best correction?
options: Award the job privately to avoid paperwork.
Ask unrelated personal questions to justify the preference.
Use consistent job-related criteria, record evidence and manage the conflict of interest.
Treat friendship as proof of occupational competence.
questions.explanation: Fair selection compares relevant evidence consistently and addresses conflicts of interest. Structured questions and documented scoring make the recommendation more defensible.

title: Business Studies · Grade 12 · Term 2: Leadership, quality and investments · Set A
subject: Business Studies

questions.question: A manager consults team members before deciding. Which leadership style best fits?
questions.explanation: Democratic leadership involves participation and consultation. It does not mean every decision must be unanimous.

questions.question: In the PDCA quality cycle, what follows Plan?
questions.explanation: Plan–Do–Check–Act means test the plan, evaluate results and act on learning. Improvement should use evidence from the check stage.

questions.question: Why should an investor compare risk and return?
options: High advertised returns remove all risk
Higher potential returns may involve greater risk of loss
questions.explanation: Risk, expected return, liquidity and time horizon affect suitability. A high return claim alone is insufficient for a decision.

questions.question: Which statement describes insurance pooling?
options: Every premium is returned in full every month
Every loss is covered without exclusions
Insurers remove every possible business risk
Many policyholders' premiums help fund covered claims subject to policy terms
questions.explanation: Pooling spreads specified risks. Coverage, exclusions, excesses and other terms determine what a claim can pay.

questions.question: An investor is promised a guaranteed exceptionally high return with no risk and pressured to pay today. Which response is strongest?
options: Pay immediately because a guarantee removes all risk.
Judge safety by the advert's expensive design alone.
Verify the provider, terms and risk independently before committing.
Borrow more because high returns cannot involve losses.
questions.explanation: Unusually high guaranteed returns and pressure justify scrutiny. Compare credible information about risk, liquidity, fees and legitimacy; a promotional promise is not independent evidence of safety.

title: Business Studies · Grade 12 · Term 3: Human rights, responsibility and presentations · Set A
subject: Business Studies

questions.question: A business installs an accessible entrance and adapts tasks for a qualified worker with a disability. Which principle is supported?
questions.explanation: Removing unnecessary barriers helps people participate fairly. Accommodation should respond to the worker's needs and job context.

questions.question: What does the triple bottom line consider?
questions.explanation: A broader assessment considers social, environmental and economic performance. Financial results alone do not show all effects of business activity.

questions.question: Which example most clearly represents a CSI project?
options: Pricing stock for a normal sale
Funding and equipping a community learning centre
questions.explanation: Corporate social investment involves resources committed to community-development initiatives. Evaluate outcomes and sustainability, not just spending.

questions.question: Why state the source and date of a chart in a presentation?
options: So the audience can judge relevance and verify the evidence
To make every old figure current
To guarantee the chart is unbiased
questions.explanation: Source and date help the audience assess credibility and currency. The presenter must still explain methods, units and limitations.

questions.question: A firm funds a community centre but ignores complaints about unsafe waste disposal. Which assessment fits the triple bottom line?
options: Only the size of the donation matters.
The CSI project does not remove the need to address environmental and social harms.
Community benefits automatically cancel every environmental cost.
questions.explanation: People, planet and profit must all be considered. Assess the centre's benefit alongside the firm's operating impacts and require evidence of corrective environmental action.

title: Business Studies · Grade 12 · Term 4: Integrated business decision revision · Set A
subject: Business Studies

questions.question: A new law raises compliance costs for all firms. Which environment is the main source of this change?
questions.explanation: Legislation is part of the wider macro environment. Businesses may influence policy collectively but cannot directly control it.

questions.question: A SWOT analysis identifies a firm's strong customer service. Which category is it?
questions.explanation: A strength is an internal advantage. Opportunities and threats arise mainly outside the business.

questions.question: Why can limited liability matter when choosing a company form?
options: Shareholders' exposure is generally limited, subject to legal exceptions
It guarantees company debts never exist
It prevents every director from any liability
It means no records are needed
questions.explanation: Limited liability generally separates company obligations from shareholders, but legal exceptions and directors' duties still matter.

questions.question: A quality programme raises costs but reduces returns and customer complaints. What should management evaluate?
options: Total costs and benefits using evidence over time
Only the colour of the quality poster
Assume fewer complaints prove every product is perfect
questions.explanation: Evaluate prevention, inspection, defect costs and customer outcomes together. A single metric does not establish the overall effect.

questions.question: A SWOT lists a new competitor as a weakness and poor staff training as a threat. Which correction is justified?
options: Both belong under strengths because they can be improved.
Both are opportunities because every change is beneficial.
The competitor is an external threat; inadequate training is an internal weakness.
Training is always external and competition always internal.
questions.explanation: SWOT distinguishes internal capabilities from external conditions. A competing firm is external, while the business's own staff-development gap is internal; the distinction guides suitable responses.

title: Economics · Grade 10 · Term 2: Markets, intervention and scarcity · Set A
subject: Economics

questions.question: If demand rises while supply is unchanged, what happens to equilibrium price in the standard model?
questions.explanation: A rightward demand shift raises equilibrium price and quantity, other things equal. Distinguish a shift from movement along a demand curve.

questions.question: A binding maximum price is set below equilibrium. What may result?
questions.explanation: At the lower price, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied. A price ceiling can create a shortage if it is binding.

questions.question: What does a point inside a production possibility curve indicate?
options: The economy is producing beyond current capacity
Resources are unemployed or used inefficiently
All resources are fully efficient by definition
questions.explanation: Inside the PPC, more output may be possible using existing resources better. A point beyond the curve requires greater capacity or technology.

questions.question: Why do economic choices have opportunity costs?
options: Choosing one option can mean giving up the next best alternative
Money is the only scarce resource
questions.explanation: Scarcity creates trade-offs. Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative forgone, which need not be a cash payment.

questions.question: A binding maximum price reduces the legal price but creates a shortage. Which evaluation recognises the trade-off?
options: Every buyer is guaranteed the same quantity at the lower price.
The shortage proves demand has disappeared.
Some buyers pay less, but availability and non-price rationing must also be assessed.
A maximum below equilibrium necessarily creates a surplus.
questions.explanation: At the controlled price quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied in the standard model. Assess access, queues and possible supply responses alongside the price paid by successful buyers.

title: Economics · Grade 10 · Term 3: Development, population and labour · Set A
subject: Economics

questions.question: What is a main benefit of a generally accepted medium of exchange over barter?
options: It reduces the need for a double coincidence of wants
questions.explanation: Money allows people to sell to one person and buy from another without each wanting exactly the other's goods.

questions.question: A country has 40 births and 25 deaths per 1 000 people, ignoring migration. Find its natural increase per 1 000.
questions.explanation: Natural increase = birth rate−death rate = 40−25=15 per 1 000. Migration is a separate component of population change.

questions.question: Why is education relevant to labour productivity?
options: It guarantees every worker a job
It can develop knowledge and skills that improve output per worker
It eliminates differences between all occupations
questions.explanation: Human-capital development can support productivity, alongside health, technology and work organisation. It does not by itself guarantee employment.

questions.question: Which action is part of collective bargaining?
options: A firm hides wages from every worker
A worker guesses the inflation rate
Worker representatives and employers negotiate employment conditions
questions.explanation: Collective bargaining involves representatives negotiating employment matters. Its outcomes depend on the process and applicable framework.

questions.question: Training raises output per worker, but employment does not immediately rise. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Training must have failed because employment was unchanged.
Output per worker and worker numbers are the same measure.
Productivity can improve without a simultaneous increase in the number employed.
The result proves training always reduces employment.
questions.explanation: Productivity concerns output relative to inputs, not simply the number of jobs. Demand, investment and business conditions also influence hiring, so separate these indicators when evaluating the programme.

title: Economics · Grade 10 · Term 4: Unemployment and economic redress · Set A
subject: Economics

questions.question: A labour force has 800 employed and 200 unemployed people. Find the unemployment rate using this definition.
questions.explanation: Labour force = employed+unemployed = 1 000. Rate = 200/1 000×100=20%. Do not divide only by those employed.

questions.question: Which situation best illustrates structural unemployment?
options: A worker voluntarily takes one lunch break
Workers' skills do not match the jobs available after industry changes
A firm changes its stationery colour
questions.explanation: Structural unemployment involves a mismatch between labour supply and demand, including skills or location. Retraining may be part of a response.

questions.question: Why might public works programmes help address unemployment?
options: They guarantee permanent jobs for everyone
They eliminate the need for training
They can provide temporary paid work and useful infrastructure
questions.explanation: Public works can provide income and assets while broader employment measures develop. Their scale, duration and training content affect their impact.

questions.question: What is an aim of economic redress?
options: Address exclusion and unequal access to economic opportunities
Ban every form of economic participation
Guarantee identical outcomes without any policy evaluation
questions.explanation: Redress aims to improve fair access and participation. Policies need evidence, implementation and evaluation rather than assuming aims guarantee success.

questions.question: A labour force has 800 employed and 200 unemployed. Fifty unemployed people stop seeking work and leave this defined labour force. What happens to the rate?
options: It stays 20% because population cannot change.
It falls to 0% because all unemployment ended.
It falls to about 15.8%, although no additional person got a job.
It rises to 25% because jobs were created.
questions.explanation: Using the stated labour-force definition, unemployment is now 150 and labour force 950: 150/950≈15.8%. The fall reflects withdrawal rather than job creation, so interpretation matters.

title: Economics · Grade 11 · Term 2: Costs, revenue and elasticity · Set A
subject: Economics

questions.question: A business sells 100 units at R20 each. Find total revenue.
questions.explanation: Total revenue = price×quantity = 20×100=R2 000. Profit requires deducting costs, which are not provided here.

questions.question: Total cost rises from R500 to R560 when output rises from 10 to 12 units. Find marginal cost per extra unit over this change.
questions.explanation: Marginal cost = change in total cost/change in quantity = 60/2=R30 per unit for this interval.

questions.question: Price rises by 10% and quantity demanded falls by 20%. Find the magnitude of price elasticity using these percentage changes.
questions.explanation: Elasticity magnitude = 20/10=2, so demand is elastic. The signed ratio is negative, but the question explicitly asks for magnitude.

questions.question: If demand is price elastic, what usually happens to total revenue after a small price cut, other things equal?
questions.explanation: The percentage quantity increase exceeds the percentage price decrease, so total revenue increases within the elastic range.

questions.question: A shop cuts price from R20 to R18 and sales rise from 100 to 120 units. Which revenue judgement is correct?
options: Revenue falls because every price cut lowers revenue.
Revenue stays R2 000 because quantity does not affect it.
Revenue rises from R2 000 to R2 160, consistent with elastic demand over this change.
Revenue rises to R2 400 because the old price still applies.
questions.explanation: Revenue is price times quantity: 20×100=2 000 and 18×120=2 160. The 20% quantity rise exceeds the 10% price fall using initial-value percentages.

title: Economics · Grade 11 · Term 3: Growth, development and banking · Set A
subject: Economics

questions.question: Which best distinguishes economic development from economic growth?
options: Growth means only a higher population
Development includes living conditions and structural improvements, beyond output growth
questions.explanation: Growth concerns increased real output. Development considers broader changes such as living standards, capabilities and economic structure.

questions.question: Why use real GDP instead of nominal GDP to compare output over time?
options: It removes all population differences automatically
questions.explanation: Real GDP uses constant prices to help separate output changes from inflation. Per-capita measures additionally consider population.

questions.question: Which is a technical function of money?
options: A replacement for every production input
questions.explanation: Money can serve as medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value. Inflation can reduce its purchasing power over time.

questions.question: Why do commercial banks assess borrowers before lending?
options: To guarantee no loan can ever default
To remove the need for contracts
To evaluate repayment ability and credit risk
To lend every deposit to one person
questions.explanation: Credit assessment supports prudent lending and risk management, though it cannot eliminate defaults.

questions.question: Nominal GDP rises 8% while the relevant price index rises 10%. Which claim needs correction?
options: That price changes affect nominal comparisons.
That real GDP helps distinguish price and output changes.
That real output necessarily grew because nominal GDP increased.
That development includes more than GDP alone.
questions.explanation: A nominal increase can be explained by higher prices. Under these indices the real factor is 1.08/1.10<1, suggesting a decline rather than proof of real growth.

title: Economics · Grade 11 · Term 4: Globalisation and environmental sustainability · Set A
subject: Economics

questions.question: Which change can promote globalisation?
options: Ending every form of international communication
questions.explanation: Lower costs make cross-border trade, investment and communication easier. Effects differ across industries and households.

questions.question: What is a negative externality of factory air pollution?
options: Only the factory's paid wage bill
A health cost borne by nearby residents that is not fully included in the factory's private costs
A benefit paid directly to every resident
questions.explanation: An external cost affects third parties outside the market transaction. Policy may seek to make decision-makers account for it.

questions.question: Which action supports sustainable resource use?
options: Use every renewable resource faster than it regenerates
Treat pollution as having no cost
Harvest at a rate that allows replenishment while protecting ecosystems
questions.explanation: Sustainability considers current needs, ecosystem limits and future needs. Renewable does not mean unlimited at any rate of use.

questions.question: Why evaluate both benefits and costs of trade openness?
options: Every person gains the same amount immediately
Trade has no effect on jobs
Only imports matter to an economy
Gains and adjustment costs can fall unevenly across groups
questions.explanation: Trade can support choice, specialisation and markets while creating adjustment pressures. Distribution and support policies matter.

questions.question: A factory creates jobs but imposes unpriced health costs on neighbours. Which policy appraisal is strongest?
options: Ignore health costs because they are outside the factory's accounts.
Close every factory without considering alternatives.
Compare employment benefits and external health costs, and assess measures that reduce pollution efficiently.
Treat all private costs as identical to all social costs.
questions.explanation: A negative externality means some costs fall on third parties. A reasoned appraisal considers both benefits and social costs, including the effectiveness and consequences of corrective measures.

title: Economics · Grade 12 · Term 2: Market structures, failure and trade · Set A
subject: Economics

questions.question: In perfect competition, an individual firm is generally a…
options: Setter of the market price independently
questions.explanation: A small firm sells an identical product in a market with many buyers and sellers, so it takes the market price in the model.

questions.question: What distinguishes an oligopoly?
options: Unlimited identical firms with no influence
A small number of interdependent large firms
No barriers to entry in every case
questions.explanation: With a few significant firms, each firm's actions affect rivals' choices. Strategic interdependence is a key feature.

questions.question: Why may public goods be underprovided by private markets?
options: They are always rival in consumption
They must be free to produce
No one receives any benefit from them
Non-excludability can create a free-rider problem
questions.explanation: If people cannot easily be excluded from benefits, collecting payment is difficult. This can weaken private incentives to supply the socially desirable quantity.

questions.question: What is a tariff?
options: A quota on how many workers can apply
A ban on all domestic production
A guaranteed subsidy to every consumer
questions.explanation: Import tariffs raise the cost of imported goods and can protect domestic producers, but may raise consumer costs and invite retaliation.

questions.question: A town relies on one water supplier with high fixed infrastructure costs. Why is counting firms alone insufficient to recommend breaking it into many suppliers?
options: More firms always guarantee lower total infrastructure costs.
A monopoly can never require regulation.
Cost structure, economies of scale, service access and regulation also affect the best arrangement.
questions.explanation: Market structure must be considered alongside costs and public-interest outcomes. Duplicating networks may be costly, while regulation and accountability can address price, access and quality concerns.

title: Economics · Grade 12 · Term 3: Inflation, indicators and sustainable tourism · Set A
subject: Economics

questions.question: A price index rises from 120 to 126. Find the inflation rate for the period.
questions.explanation: Inflation = (126−120)/120×100=5%. The six index points are not six percent of the original index.

questions.question: What can cause demand-pull inflation?
options: A fall in every source of demand
A guaranteed fall in the money supply alone
Aggregate demand grows faster than available real output at capacity
questions.explanation: Pressure from total spending can bid up prices when real output cannot expand sufficiently. Distinguish this from cost-push pressures.

questions.question: Why is tourism described as having a multiplier effect?
options: Tourist spending generates further income and spending in connected activities
Every rand automatically doubles exactly once
All spending stays inside one hotel
Imports do not affect any tourism income
questions.explanation: Initial spending supports incomes, some of which are spent again. Saving, taxes and imports are leakages that affect the size of the effect.

questions.question: Which indicator combines health, education and income dimensions?
questions.explanation: HDI combines life expectancy, education and income measures. It complements economic output indicators rather than measuring every aspect of well-being.

questions.question: The inflation rate falls from 8% to 5%, remaining positive. A learner says average prices have fallen. Which correction is right?
options: Prices must fall by 3% because the rate fell by three points.
All goods now have unchanged prices.
Prices are rising more slowly; a lower positive inflation rate is not a fall in the price level.
questions.explanation: Inflation is the rate of increase of the general price level. A fall in that positive rate is disinflation, while a falling general price level would require negative inflation.

title: Economics · Grade 12 · Term 4: Integrated macro- and microeconomics revision · Set A
subject: Economics

questions.question: In a simplified closed economy without government, MPC = 0.8. Find the expenditure multiplier.
questions.explanation: k=1/(1−MPC)=1/0.2=5 under the stated assumptions. A more complex economy has additional leakages.

questions.question: Why does real GDP per capita provide more context than total real GDP alone?
options: It relates real output to population size
It measures every household's exact income
questions.explanation: Divide real GDP by population. An average helps comparison but does not show how income is distributed.

questions.question: If the rand depreciates against the dollar, what happens to the rand price of a fixed dollar import price, all else equal?
questions.explanation: A weaker rand means more rand are needed for each dollar. Actual prices may also depend on contracts, taxes and other costs.

questions.question: Which policy response most directly addresses a negative production externality in the textbook model?
options: Paying firms more for extra pollution without conditions
A well-designed pollution charge linked to external costs
questions.explanation: A charge can internalise external costs and influence production choices. Design, enforcement and distributional effects determine real-world results.

questions.question: In a simplified multiplier model MPC=0.8 gives k=5. Why should a R1 million injection not be treated as a guaranteed R5 million real-output increase in practice?
options: The model proves unlimited resources exist.
A multiplier of five means every household receives R5 million.
Leakages, capacity limits, imports and behavioural responses can change the outcome.
Government spending can never affect demand.
questions.explanation: The simple model rests on restrictive assumptions. Real economies have taxes, imports, saving changes and capacity constraints, so its predicted total effect needs contextual qualification.

title: Geography · Grade 10 · Term 2: Plate tectonics and geological hazards · Set A
subject: Geography

questions.question: At a constructive plate boundary, plates generally…
options: Move apart and new crust can form
Move towards one another in every case
questions.explanation: Divergent plate movement can allow magma to rise and solidify as new crust. Identify the boundary type before predicting processes.

questions.question: Which rock forms when magma or lava cools and solidifies?
options: Any rock only after fossils form
questions.explanation: Igneous rocks form through cooling of molten material. Sedimentary and metamorphic rocks form through different processes.

questions.question: What is the focus of an earthquake?
options: The point directly above it on the surface
The point inside Earth where rupture begins
questions.explanation: The focus, or hypocentre, is within Earth. The epicentre is the surface point directly above it.

questions.question: Why can similar earthquakes cause different losses in two cities?
options: Magnitude is the only possible factor
Exposure, building quality and preparedness differ
questions.explanation: Risk depends on the hazard plus vulnerability and exposure. Safer buildings and preparation can reduce losses without preventing earthquakes.

questions.question: Two cities experience similar earthquakes but different losses. Which comparison best investigates the difference?
options: Only the spelling of each city's name.
Magnitude alone, assuming all other factors are identical.
Building standards, population exposure, ground conditions and preparedness in both cities.
A single photograph without its location.
questions.explanation: Hazard magnitude does not determine losses alone. Compare vulnerability and exposure with relevant physical conditions before attributing the different impacts to one cause.

title: Geography · Grade 10 · Term 3: Population geography and migration · Set A
subject: Geography

questions.question: A district has 60 000 people in 200 km². Find its population density.
questions.explanation: Population density = population/area = 60 000/200 = 300 people per km². An average can hide uneven distribution.

questions.question: What may a broad base on a population pyramid suggest?
options: A large proportion of young people
All age groups have equal numbers
questions.explanation: The base represents younger ages. Interpret the full pyramid and data context before predicting future growth.

questions.question: Which is a push factor for migration?
options: Access to a desired university elsewhere
questions.explanation: Push factors encourage departure from an origin. Pull factors attract people towards a destination.

questions.question: Why can rural–urban migration create planning challenges?
options: Services and housing may need to expand rapidly
It automatically reduces all urban populations
It means every migrant has the same experience
questions.explanation: Rapid population change can increase demand for housing, water, transport and jobs. Planning should consider varied needs and contributions.

questions.question: A district's density is 300 people/km². A planner concludes every square kilometre contains exactly 300 people. What is wrong?
options: Density states every household has 300 members.
Averages can only be used for temperature.
Density is an average; settlement can be uneven within the district.
The land area must equal the population.
questions.explanation: Total population divided by area gives an average, not a uniform distribution. Maps of settlement and land use are needed to plan local services.

title: Geography · Grade 10 · Term 4: Water management and flooding · Set A
subject: Geography

questions.question: Why can paving land increase rapid surface runoff?
options: Less water infiltrates through impermeable surfaces
Every paved area prevents all flooding
questions.explanation: Impermeable surfaces reduce infiltration and can speed runoff to drains and rivers. Drainage capacity and rainfall intensity also matter.

questions.question: Which action most directly supports sustainable school water use?
options: Leave taps running to test the pipes
Use treated drinking water for every unnecessary task
questions.explanation: Fixing leaks reduces avoidable losses. Monitoring shows whether savings persist and helps detect new problems.

questions.question: Why protect vegetation in a river catchment?
options: It can slow runoff, support infiltration and reduce erosion
It guarantees no flood can ever occur
It prevents all water reaching rivers
questions.explanation: Vegetation helps regulate water movement and stabilise soil. Flood risk also depends on storm intensity, saturation and land use.

questions.question: What is a key concern when building homes on a floodplain?
options: The river can never change level
Only the paint colour of houses
questions.explanation: Floodplains are areas rivers can inundate. Site selection, warnings and flood management should account for this recurring risk.

questions.question: A town proposes a higher river wall as its only flood measure. Which appraisal is most complete?
options: Assume any wall eliminates every future flood.
Ignore upstream land use because rivers are isolated at town borders.
Assess the wall alongside upstream runoff, floodplain exposure, maintenance and warning systems.
Move warnings to after flood damage is recorded.
questions.explanation: Flood risk depends on catchment processes, infrastructure and exposure. A combined appraisal considers effectiveness, displaced risk and maintenance rather than treating one structure as a universal solution.

title: Geography · Grade 11 · Term 2: Rock structure, slopes and mass movement · Set A
subject: Geography

questions.question: A cuesta forms in strata with a gentle dip. Which slopes typically characterise it?
options: A flat surface with no slope
A steep scarp slope and a gentler dip slope
questions.explanation: Differential erosion of tilted resistant and less-resistant layers can produce an asymmetric ridge. The dip slope follows bedding inclination.

questions.question: What is soil creep?
options: Very slow downslope movement of soil
questions.explanation: Soil creep is a slow mass movement under gravity. Bent trunks or tilted posts can provide evidence over time.

questions.question: Why can heavy rain increase landslide risk on a vulnerable slope?
options: Water can add weight and reduce material strength
questions.explanation: Saturation can increase load and pore pressure, reducing stability. Slope material, angle and vegetation affect the risk.

questions.question: On a topographic map, closely spaced contours generally indicate…
options: A greater scale denominator by definition
questions.explanation: For a constant contour interval, the same vertical change occurs over a shorter horizontal distance, indicating a steeper slope.

questions.question: A steep slope is cut for a road and later fails after heavy rain. Which explanation best integrates the evidence?
options: Rainfall proves road cutting had no possible role.
Slope failure must be caused by one factor only.
Cutting may reduce support while rain increases saturation and reduces stability.
The road's painted line determines soil strength.
questions.explanation: Slope instability can reflect interacting natural and human factors. Investigate geology, drainage, slope geometry and the timing of cutting and rainfall before assigning responsibility.

title: Geography · Grade 11 · Term 3: Development, trade and aid · Set A
subject: Geography

questions.question: Why use more than GDP per capita when comparing development?
options: Development includes health, education and distribution as well as income
GDP per capita proves everyone earns the average
questions.explanation: Development is multidimensional. Combine income with social indicators and consider inequality and local context.

questions.question: Which is an example of humanitarian aid?
options: A routine export sale at market price
Emergency food and shelter after a disaster
A tax paid by a local shop
A share purchase by an investor
questions.explanation: Humanitarian aid addresses urgent needs and protects people in crises. Longer-term development assistance has different but sometimes connected aims.

questions.question: Why might reliance on one export commodity be risky?
options: Trade becomes completely independent of world markets
Global price changes can strongly affect income
questions.explanation: Concentrated exports expose earnings to price and demand shocks. Diversification can reduce, though not eliminate, vulnerability.

questions.question: What makes a development project more community-responsive?
options: Outsiders assume every community has identical needs
Local people help identify needs, decide priorities and evaluate outcomes
questions.explanation: Participation can improve relevance and accountability. Results should be evaluated with the people affected, not inferred from spending alone.

questions.question: Two countries have equal GDP per capita, but different life expectancy and schooling. Which judgement is justified?
options: All development measures must therefore be identical.
The country with less schooling necessarily has more income.
Equal average income does not establish equal development or distribution.
Health measures cannot inform development comparisons.
questions.explanation: GDP per capita is an average economic indicator. Health, education, inequality and access can differ, so use several indicators before judging development.

title: Geography · Grade 11 · Term 4: Energy management and soil erosion · Set A
subject: Geography

questions.question: Which energy source is renewable on a human timescale?
questions.explanation: Sunlight is replenished continuously on human timescales. Fossil fuels form over geological timescales and are finite.

questions.question: What is a major environmental cost of coal-fired electricity?
options: Greenhouse gas emissions and air pollutants
questions.explanation: Coal combustion releases greenhouse gases and other pollutants. Full assessment also considers mining, water and management practices.

questions.question: How can overgrazing increase soil erosion?
options: It always increases protective plant cover
It reduces vegetation cover, exposing soil to wind and runoff
questions.explanation: Loss of plant cover and roots leaves soil less protected. Grazing management should account for carrying capacity and recovery.

questions.question: Which action best supports household energy efficiency?
options: Use efficient appliances and switch off unnecessary loads
Leave all heaters on in empty rooms
questions.explanation: Efficiency reduces energy needed for a service. Combine efficient equipment, maintenance and sensible use, then check actual consumption.

questions.question: An overgrazed hillside loses more soil than a vegetated one after storms. What investigation best tests vegetation's role?
options: Compare unrelated slopes without measuring rainfall or soil.
Assume vegetation is the only possible cause.
Compare repeated soil-loss measurements on similar slopes with different cover, controlling other factors.
Use only a photograph taken before rain.
questions.explanation: Similar slopes, soil and rainfall reduce competing explanations. Repeated measurements can reveal whether cover is associated with reduced runoff and erosion more reliably than a single observation.

title: Geography · Grade 12 · Term 2: Fluvial processes and settlements · Set A
subject: Geography

questions.question: What is river rejuvenation?
options: A river ceasing every process permanently
The automatic creation of a lake at every mouth
Renewed erosive energy, often following a fall in base level or land uplift
A river becoming older by one year
questions.explanation: A change in relative base level or gradient can renew vertical erosion. Features can include incised meanders or knickpoints.

questions.question: What is rural–urban migration?
options: Every daily trip to a shop
Movement of people from rural areas to towns and cities
questions.explanation: Rural–urban migration changes residence and can affect both origin and destination. Do not confuse it with daily commuting.

questions.question: Which factor commonly helps explain a settlement's original site?
options: Access to water and a suitable location for activities
A guarantee of future industrial growth
questions.explanation: A site is the physical location and its characteristics. Situation concerns its relative location and connections to other places.

questions.question: Why may informal settlements develop rapidly near cities?
options: Affordable formal housing may not keep pace with migration and household formation
Urban housing demand is always zero
They occur only where no jobs exist
questions.explanation: Housing supply, land access, incomes and population change interact. Avoid explanations that blame residents or assume one universal cause.

questions.question: A city relocates informal households far from jobs without reliable transport. Which evaluation considers settlement needs most fully?
options: New buildings alone guarantee improved access to livelihoods.
Assess housing quality together with affordability, livelihoods, transport and community participation.
Exclude residents because only building counts matter.
questions.explanation: Settlement policy affects daily access and costs as well as structures. A stronger appraisal includes residents' priorities and the feasibility of reaching work, schools and services.

title: Geography · Grade 12 · Term 3: South Africa's economic geography · Set A
subject: Geography

questions.question: Which activity belongs to the primary sector?
questions.explanation: The primary sector extracts or produces raw materials. Steelmaking transforms them in the secondary sector.

questions.question: Why can transport infrastructure influence industrial location?
options: It affects access to inputs, markets and distribution costs
All transport costs are identical everywhere
It removes the need for labour
questions.explanation: Transport is one location factor alongside labour, power, water, land and policy. Different industries weigh these differently.

questions.question: Which best describes small-scale subsistence farming?

Production mainly for the household's own use
A guarantee of no surplus in any year

questions.question: Why do mining benefits need to be assessed alongside costs?

questions.question: A proposed mine promises jobs but threatens a river used by downstream farms. Which evidence is needed for a balanced decision?
options: Only the promoter's projected job number.
Only a promotional photograph of machinery.
Credible employment estimates and environmental, water-use and community-impact assessments.
An assumption that economic benefits erase all environmental costs.
questions.explanation: Economic geography weighs benefits and costs across places and groups. Investigate water impacts, mitigation and who gains or bears risks alongside employment and revenue.

title: Geography · Grade 12 · Term 4: Climate, drainage and map-skill revision · Set A
subject: Geography

questions.question: On a 1:50 000 map, two points are 4 cm apart. Find straight-line ground distance.
questions.explanation: 4×50 000 = 200 000 cm = 2 km. A route distance may be longer than the straight-line distance.

questions.question: What does a drainage basin include?
options: The area drained by a river and its tributaries
Every ocean connected to any river
questions.explanation: Watershed boundaries separate drainage basins. Water within a basin generally drains towards its river system.

questions.question: What often happens where warm, moist air rises up a mountain slope?
options: It cools, may condense and can produce orographic rain
Every cloud evaporates regardless of conditions
questions.explanation: Rising air expands and cools. If it reaches saturation, condensation can form cloud and precipitation on the windward slope.

questions.question: Why interpret a map together with its key and scale?
options: All maps use identical symbols and scales
The key replaces all spatial thinking
Symbols and distances need their stated meanings and units
questions.explanation: A key explains symbols and a scale links map distance to ground distance. Read both before identifying features or measuring.

questions.question: Two points are 2 km apart in a straight line on a map. A learner says the walking route must take 20 minutes at 6 km/h. Why is this uncertain?
options: Map scale guarantees every route is flat.
Walking speed cannot be related to distance.
The path may be longer or steeper than the straight-line distance.
questions.explanation: The 20-minute calculation assumes a 2 km route at constant 6 km/h. Actual paths, contours, obstacles and stops may change distance and speed; use route and relief information.

title: History · Grade 10 · Term 2: French Revolution and historical reasoning · Set A
subject: History

questions.question: Which condition contributed to revolutionary pressures in France before 1789?
options: Universal equal taxation already accepted by all
Financial crisis and unequal burdens within the estate system
A fully democratic republic for centuries
questions.explanation: Fiscal crisis, privilege, inequality and new political ideas contributed to tensions. A strong answer explains their interaction rather than listing only one cause.

questions.question: What did the slogan liberty, equality and fraternity express in the French Revolution?
options: A promise that inequality ended immediately everywhere
Ideals challenging aspects of the old political and social order
questions.explanation: The slogan expressed revolutionary ideals. Examine how far different groups experienced those ideals in practice.

questions.question: A historian studies a speech by a revolutionary leader. What should be considered?
options: Only whether its handwriting looks attractive
That a speech must be neutral
That political speeches are always useless
Its author, audience, purpose and context
questions.explanation: A source's purpose and audience shape what it reveals and what it may omit. Bias affects interpretation but does not automatically make it useless.

questions.question: Why do historians compare accounts of political change in southern Africa after 1750?
options: Different evidence and perspectives can challenge single-cause explanations
All oral accounts must be discarded
The first published account must always be accepted
questions.explanation: Comparison and corroboration help evaluate contested interpretations. Consider chronology, context and the strengths and limits of different evidence.

questions.question: A revolutionary leader's speech claims everyone supported reform. Which use of the source is most defensible?
options: Treat everyone as literally unanimous because the speaker said so.
Discard the source because political speakers have purposes.
Use it to study the leader's aims and rhetoric, then compare evidence from other groups.
Use the speech to establish events centuries later without context.
questions.explanation: A purposeful speech can reveal ideology and persuasion but cannot alone establish universal support. Corroboration and context help evaluate the scope of its claims.

title: History · Grade 10 · Term 3: Colonial expansion, war and Union · Set A
subject: History

questions.question: What was one effect of colonial expansion into the interior of southern Africa?
options: Equal political rights for all inhabitants
Changes to land control and labour relations
questions.explanation: Expansion affected land, labour, political authority and resistance. Effects varied across places and communities and should be supported with examples.

questions.question: Why is mining capitalism relevant to studying the South African War?
options: The war had no economic context
Every cause can be reduced to one mine owner
Gold, capital and competing political interests shaped tensions
questions.explanation: Economic change helps explain tensions, alongside political and imperial factors. Avoid presenting one factor as the only cause.

questions.question: A source is a civilian's diary written during a war. What can it reveal especially well?
options: That individual's experiences and perceptions at the time
A complete neutral account of every battlefield
The intentions of every government leader
The experiences of all civilians without comparison
questions.explanation: A diary provides a situated perspective. It may be valuable for lived experience while needing comparison with other sources for broader claims.

questions.question: What is a sound historical paragraph?
options: A clear point supported by relevant evidence and explanation
A copied source with no interpretation
questions.explanation: Link the point, evidence and reasoning to the question. Evidence matters because it supports, qualifies or challenges the argument.

questions.question: A wartime diary describes food shortages in one household. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: It proves every household had identical shortages.
A personal source has no historical value.
It provides evidence of that household's experience; wider claims need comparison.
The writer necessarily knew all military decisions.
questions.explanation: A contemporary diary offers detailed lived experience from a particular perspective. Its reach is limited, so compare other testimonies and records before generalising nationally.

title: History · Grade 10 · Term 4: The 1913 land law and examination skills · Set A
subject: History

questions.question: What was a major effect of the Natives Land Act of 1913?
options: Providing equal land access to all
Giving every family an equal farm
Restricting African land acquisition and occupation along racial lines
questions.explanation: The law entrenched discriminatory land restrictions with major economic and social consequences. Use its historical context to explain later patterns.

questions.question: Why is Sol Plaatje's writing useful for studying the 1913 land law?
options: It records an informed contemporary critique and experiences of its effects
It is automatically free of viewpoint
It proves every person had the same experience
questions.explanation: Plaatje offers valuable contemporary evidence. Evaluate his purpose and corroborate specific claims rather than treating any source as complete.

questions.question: What does corroborating a source mean?
options: Checking its claims against other relevant evidence
questions.explanation: Corroboration compares evidence for support or contradiction. Independent sources and context help assess reliability.

questions.question: An essay asks to what extent a policy changed society. What must the answer do?
options: Evaluate the degree of change with evidence and qualifications
Avoid evidence that complicates the argument
questions.explanation: An extent judgment weighs change and continuity and reaches a supported conclusion. Address counter-evidence rather than ignoring it.

questions.question: An essay claims the 1913 land law had identical effects on every African family immediately. What would strengthen the argument?
options: Repeat the word identical without additional evidence.
Use only the law's title as proof of every outcome.
Examine varied regional and household experiences and qualify the scope of change.
Ignore experiences that complicate the claim.
questions.explanation: Legislation and implementation can affect groups differently. A strong historical judgement relates the law's racial restrictions to evidence of actual outcomes and acknowledges variation.

title: History · Grade 11 · Term 2: Ideas of race and nationalisms · Set A
subject: History

questions.question: Why are nineteenth-century racial hierarchies rejected by modern understandings of humanity?
options: They are discriminatory social constructions, not a valid ranking of human worth or ability
They accurately rank every person's potential
They prove separate unequal human species
questions.explanation: Historical racist ideas helped justify exclusion and violence. Modern evidence does not support ranking human populations by inherent worth or ability.

questions.question: What did eugenic policies attempt to do?
options: Provide equal reproductive freedom to everyone
Control reproduction using discriminatory ideas about inherited human value
questions.explanation: Eugenics used harmful claims about heredity to justify coercion and exclusion. Explain and critique the ideas without endorsing them.

questions.question: What is nationalism in a historical context?
options: A belief that all states must disappear immediately
Identification with a nation and claims linked to its political interests or self-determination
Only a preference for a sports team
questions.explanation: Nationalisms develop in particular contexts and can unite, exclude or challenge domination. Compare concrete movements rather than assuming all are identical.

questions.question: Why compare sources from different nationalist movements?
options: To prove every movement had identical goals
To assume one source speaks for all members
To examine similarities, differences and the circumstances shaping each
questions.explanation: Comparative work needs evidence about aims, leadership, membership and context, including tensions within movements.

questions.question: A nationalist pamphlet describes its own movement as representing the entire population. Which evaluation is best?
options: Assume a pamphlet's claim proves universal representation.
Reject all nationalist sources without reading them.
Compare its aims and audience with evidence of support, exclusion and rival views.
Use modern popularity alone to establish past support.
questions.explanation: Representation is a claim to investigate. The pamphlet reveals the movement's self-presentation, while other sources help assess who supported it and whose interests it excluded.

title: History · Grade 11 · Term 3: Segregation and the apartheid state · Set A
subject: History

questions.question: What distinguishes apartheid as a state policy after 1948?
options: The first appearance of any racism anywhere
A systematic extension and enforcement of racial segregation and unequal rights
Universal equal citizenship from its start
An immediate end to earlier segregation
questions.explanation: Apartheid built on earlier discriminatory structures while expanding and systematising them. A comparison should identify both continuity and change.

questions.question: Why did apartheid legislation affect everyday life?
options: It applied only to foreign trade
It had no relation to state power
It regulated areas such as residence, movement, education and political participation
It guaranteed equal services to all
questions.explanation: Interlocking laws enforced racial control across many parts of life. Specific examples strengthen an explanation of impact.

questions.question: What is a limitation of using a government statement alone to assess a policy's effects?
options: Government documents contain no historical information
It must describe every outcome accurately
It removes the need for other evidence
It may present official justification while omitting affected people's experiences
questions.explanation: Official sources reveal intentions and public messaging. Compare them with implementation records and affected communities' testimony.

questions.question: Why is a single-cause explanation of the 1948 election result weak?
options: It may ignore interacting political, social and electoral factors
Every historical event has exactly one cause
questions.explanation: Historical explanation should weigh several relevant factors and distinguish background conditions from immediate events.

questions.question: A government statement says a segregation policy benefits everyone. Testimony from affected families describes restrictions. What should a historian do?
options: Accept official status as proof that family accounts are false.
Assume disagreement makes both sources worthless.
Compare purpose, context and specific evidence, explaining differing perspectives.
Choose whichever source has the shorter text.
questions.explanation: Different positions shape accounts, but claims can still be investigated. Explain each source's perspective and compare its evidence with legislation and further testimony.

title: History · Grade 11 · Term 4: Resistance, repression and source skills · Set A
subject: History

questions.question: What did mass mobilisation seek to achieve in resistance to apartheid?
options: Limit action to a single secret diary
Bring many people into collective political action
questions.explanation: Mobilisation organised collective action through campaigns and networks. Its forms and effectiveness changed in response to conditions and repression.

questions.question: Why was the Sharpeville massacre in 1960 historically significant?
options: It intensified criticism of apartheid and affected the course of resistance and state repression
questions.explanation: The killing of protesters had major national and international repercussions. Explain the consequences with evidence and correct chronology.

questions.question: What was a consequence of the Rivonia Trial for the liberation movement?
options: Key leaders were imprisoned, affecting leadership and resistance strategies
Every political organisation became freely legal
questions.explanation: The trial and imprisonment of leaders reshaped the struggle. It did not end resistance, which continued through different organisations and settings.

questions.question: When two sources disagree, what should a learner do?
options: Examine perspective, date, evidence and context before judging the claims
Treat the older source as always correct
questions.explanation: Contradiction is a reason for investigation. Evaluate what each source can establish and seek additional corroborating evidence.

questions.question: Two sources give different accounts of a protest. Which approach produces the strongest source-based answer?
options: Average every number without checking how it was obtained.
Select the later source solely because it is later.
Identify precise agreements and differences, examine provenance and corroborate key claims.
Avoid all conclusions because disagreement exists.
questions.explanation: Source disagreement is evidence to analyse. Dates, access to events, purposes and corroboration help judge particular claims rather than automatically accepting or rejecting a whole source.

title: History · Grade 12 · Term 2: Black Consciousness, transition and reconciliation · Set A
subject: History

questions.question: What was a central emphasis of Black Consciousness associated with Steve Biko?
options: Withdrawal of all criticism of oppression
A claim that only legislation affects identity
Psychological liberation, dignity and self-reliance among oppressed black people
questions.explanation: Black Consciousness challenged internalised oppression and promoted agency and solidarity. Explain its context and influence using specific evidence.

questions.question: What was one purpose of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission?
options: Investigate gross human-rights violations and create a public record of testimony
Guarantee that no disagreements about the past remained
questions.explanation: The TRC sought truth-telling and reconciliation through its mandate. Amnesty required specified conditions; its outcomes and limits remain subjects of evaluation.

questions.question: How did the end of the Cold War affect South Africa's political context?
options: It alone mechanically caused every decision
It changed international pressures and strategic calculations around negotiations
It removed every domestic conflict immediately
questions.explanation: Global changes interacted with internal resistance, economic pressures and leadership decisions. Avoid treating international change as the sole cause.

questions.question: Why evaluate both achievements and limitations of reconciliation initiatives?
options: Critical evaluation is incompatible with evidence
Their aims and actual effects may differ across people and issues
All testimony gives the same experience
questions.explanation: A balanced argument compares goals, processes and outcomes, including justice, acknowledgement and unresolved material inequalities.

questions.question: A learner argues that public TRC testimony proves reconciliation was fully achieved for everyone. Which response is most defensible?
options: Assume testimony guarantees all victims received the same outcome.
Reject every testimony because reconciliation is difficult.
Distinguish the creation of a public record from the varied experiences and unresolved limits of reconciliation.
Use the commission's name as sufficient proof of complete success.
questions.explanation: An institution's aims and public proceedings are not identical to all social outcomes. Evaluate achievements and limitations with evidence from affected people and the broader context.

title: History · Grade 12 · Term 3: Globalisation and a new world order · Set A
subject: History

questions.question: What does globalisation describe?
options: Increasing cross-border connections in economies, politics, culture and communication
The end of all international interaction
questions.explanation: Globalisation has several dimensions and uneven effects. Define the dimension relevant to the question before evaluating its consequences.

questions.question: Why can globalisation affect African states differently?
options: Every state has identical resources and institutions
Economic structures, bargaining power and domestic policies vary
Geography and history have no influence
All foreign investment has identical effects
questions.explanation: Different positions in trade, finance and production shape opportunities and constraints. Support comparisons with specific evidence.

questions.question: An editorial praises an international financial policy. What should a historian investigate?
options: Who produced it, its interests, evidence and intended audience
questions.explanation: Editorials provide perspectives and arguments. Assess evidence and context, and compare with other affected groups' experiences.

questions.question: What makes an argument about a new world order convincing?
options: A list of dates with no relationship to the question
Ignoring evidence from outside one country
A supported claim that weighs change, continuity and competing interpretations
questions.explanation: A strong argument links evidence across cases to a clear judgment, while acknowledging limits and alternative interpretations.

questions.question: An editorial welcomes a global financial policy while workers' accounts describe job losses. Which synthesis is strongest?
options: Only the editorial counts because it is published.
Only negative effects can ever be historical evidence.
Evaluate the policy's different effects on groups using contextual evidence and each source's perspective.
Opposing accounts prove neither group experienced any effect.
questions.explanation: Globalisation can distribute gains and adjustment costs unevenly. Assess specific claims, interests and context to form a qualified argument rather than presume one uniform outcome.

title: History · Grade 12 · Term 4: Source-based and essay examination revision · Set A
subject: History

questions.question: A question says use the source and your own knowledge. What is required?
options: Integrate source evidence with relevant contextual knowledge
Write unrelated facts from any topic
questions.explanation: Show what the source establishes and connect it to accurate outside knowledge. Keep both relevant to the wording of the question.

questions.question: What is the best way to introduce a historical essay?
options: State a clear position responding to the question and outline its line of argument
Copy the question without adding meaning
questions.explanation: The introduction should frame the argument. The body supports it with evidence and the conclusion returns to the judgment.

questions.question: How should a learner use a political cartoon as evidence?
options: Treat every drawing as a literal photograph
Assume humour means it has no historical use
Interpret symbols and message in relation to creator, audience and historical context
questions.explanation: Cartoons compress and exaggerate viewpoints. Context and visual details help explain the message and its limitations as evidence.

questions.question: Why is chronology important in explaining historical causation?
options: A proposed cause must precede the effect and fit the wider sequence
Every earlier event caused every later event
Events after an outcome always caused it
questions.explanation: Chronology helps test causal claims, but an earlier event is not automatically a cause. Explain mechanisms and supporting evidence.

questions.question: An essay uses an event in 1965 as the cause of a policy adopted in 1960. What revision is needed?
options: Keep the claim because all related events are interchangeable.
Remove every date from the essay.
Correct the chronology and identify earlier causes; the later event may be a consequence or later development.
Treat the later event as earlier without evidence.
questions.explanation: A cause must precede its effect. Establish an accurate sequence and distinguish origins, consequences and later reinforcement before building a causal argument.

title: Tourism · Grade 10 · Term 2: Map work and domestic tourism · Set A
subject: Tourism

questions.question: A traveller visits Durban from their home in Johannesburg. What type of tourism is this?
questions.explanation: The traveller remains within their own country. Domestic tourism can cross provincial boundaries without becoming international tourism.

questions.question: What does a map legend explain?
options: The exact price of every hotel
The meaning of symbols used on that map
questions.explanation: A legend, or key, helps interpret features and services represented by symbols. Check the map's own key rather than assuming every symbol is universal.

questions.question: A route table gives 120 km from A to B and 80 km from B to C. Via B, how far is A to C?
questions.explanation: For the stated route, add the two legs: 120+80=200 km. A direct route could differ, but it is not the route specified.

questions.question: Why can domestic tourism support local economies?
options: All visitor spending goes abroad automatically
Visitor spending can support businesses, jobs and linked suppliers
It guarantees equal income for every resident
questions.explanation: Local spending can create direct and indirect benefits. Who benefits depends on ownership, sourcing and local linkages.

questions.question: A route planner chooses a 200 km route over a 160 km route because its roads are faster. What must be checked before recommending it?
options: Distance alone, because shorter always means faster.
Road conditions, likely travel time, safety, stops and visitor needs for both routes.
Only the name of the destination.
questions.explanation: Distance is only one planning factor. Compare realistic speeds, access, safety and stops to justify a route suited to travellers rather than assume a single distance measure settles the choice.

title: Tourism · Grade 10 · Term 3: Attractions and responsible tourism · Set A
subject: Tourism

questions.question: Which behaviour best protects a wildlife attraction?
options: Keep a safe distance and follow park rules
questions.explanation: Responsible visitors avoid disturbing animals and habitats. Follow local guidance and protect both people and wildlife.

questions.question: What are the three commonly used sustainability pillars?
questions.explanation: Sustainable tourism considers ecosystems, communities and economic viability together. A project can succeed financially while causing other harms.

questions.question: Why should marketing identify a target market?
options: One message always suits everyone equally
Different visitors have different needs, budgets and interests
It removes the need to research customers
It guarantees every advertisement will succeed
questions.explanation: A defined market helps choose relevant products, messages and channels. Test assumptions through research and feedback.

questions.question: A lodge buys produce from nearby farmers. What benefit can this support?
options: A guarantee of zero environmental impact
An end to every seasonal job
questions.explanation: Local purchasing can retain more visitor spending in the area and support suppliers. Sustainability still requires considering quality, fairness and environmental effects.

questions.question: A lodge calls itself sustainable because it buys local produce, but it wastes water and excludes local residents from decisions. Which evaluation is strongest?
options: One local purchase proves complete sustainability.
Water use has no place in tourism evaluation.
Local sourcing is a benefit, but environmental and social practices also need assessment.
questions.explanation: Sustainability includes environmental, social and economic dimensions. Assess actual sourcing, resource use and community participation before accepting the broad marketing claim.

title: Tourism · Grade 10 · Term 4: Culture, communication and customer care · Set A
subject: Tourism

questions.question: Why should guides avoid stereotypes when describing a community's culture?
options: Individuals and traditions are diverse and should be represented respectfully
questions.explanation: Respectful interpretation recognises diversity and changing practices. Ask, research and avoid presenting a whole community as uniform.

questions.question: A guest says their booking is wrong. What is the best first response?
options: Listen, clarify the details and check the booking record
questions.explanation: Customer care begins with listening and accurate information. Then explain practical options within the business's authority.

questions.question: Which written message is clearest for a guest?
options: Your tour departs from reception at 08:30 tomorrow; please arrive by 08:15.
questions.explanation: Useful communication specifies action, place and time. Avoid assumptions and invite clarification where needed.

questions.question: Why conserve cultural heritage?
options: It requires every tradition to stop changing
It belongs to no living community
It can protect valued knowledge, places and practices for communities and future generations
questions.explanation: Heritage conservation should respect community meaning and participation. Tourism is one use, not the sole reason heritage matters.

questions.question: A guide plans a cultural visit without asking hosts how practices should be represented. What improvement is best?
options: Use stereotypes because they make every visit simpler.
Assume payment permits every photograph and activity.
Consult hosts, obtain appropriate agreement and present accurate context respectfully.
Replace the hosts' account with invented stories.
questions.explanation: Responsible cultural tourism respects people's agency, context and boundaries. Consultation helps ensure accurate representation and appropriate visitor behaviour rather than imposing assumptions.

title: Tourism · Grade 11 · Term 2: Car rental, heritage and marketing · Set A
subject: Tourism

questions.question: Why should a traveller compare the full car-rental quote rather than only the daily rate?
options: Every quote includes unlimited free extras
Extra charges, insurance terms and mileage conditions affect total cost
The daily rate is always the final cost
questions.explanation: Check included kilometres, excesses, optional extras and other charges. A low headline rate may not be the cheapest suitable option.

questions.question: What does an insurance excess generally mean in a rental context?
options: A guaranteed refund of the whole rental
A free extra driver in every contract
The amount the renter may remain liable for under the cover's terms
questions.explanation: An excess is a potential retained liability. Read exclusions, reductions and conditions rather than assuming the renter has no risk.

questions.question: A museum promotes a community-led exhibition. What should its marketing emphasise?
options: A guarantee that all visitors share one culture
Accurate information and respectful representation of the community
questions.explanation: Cultural tourism needs accurate, respectful interpretation and appropriate permissions. Community participation strengthens authenticity and relevance.

questions.question: Which is a target-market decision?
options: Designing a short affordable itinerary for local families
Offering every product at an identical price by law
questions.explanation: Market selection informs product, price and promotion decisions. It starts with understanding the needs of a defined visitor group.

questions.question: Rental A costs R400/day plus R300 once; B costs R500/day with that fee included. For two days, excluding all other costs, which quote is cheaper?
options: A at R800, ignoring its fee.
B at R1 000, compared with A at R1 100.
B at R500 for the entire two-day hire.
questions.explanation: A totals 2×400+300=R1 100. B totals 2×500=R1 000. Compare the complete stated cost, then check mileage, cover and other terms before an actual booking.
