title: Tourism · Grade 11 · Term 3: Itineraries, exchange rates and service · Set A
subject: Tourism

questions.question: An itinerary has activities at 09:00 and 09:15 in towns 80 km apart. What is its main problem?
options: The font must be changed before anything else
Every route must cross a border
questions.explanation: An itinerary must allow realistic travel and visiting time, plus breaks and contingencies. Geographic sequence and timing should work together.

questions.question: A bank sells foreign currency at R20 per US dollar. Ignoring fees, how many dollars does R2 000 buy?
questions.explanation: Divide rand by rand per dollar: 2 000/20=100 dollars. Fees and the appropriate buying or selling rate affect real transactions.

questions.question: A tourist exchanges US$50 at R18 per dollar, with no fee. How many rand do they receive?
questions.explanation: Multiply dollars by rand per dollar: 50×18=R900. Track the units to choose multiplication or division.

questions.question: A foreign guest struggles to understand a service explanation. What should staff do?
options: Speak louder and refuse to clarify
Use clear language, check understanding and offer suitable support
questions.explanation: Respectful communication adapts language and checks the message was understood. Avoid stereotyping or treating language difficulty as lack of ability.

questions.question: A visit ends at 10:00; the next begins at 10:30, 60 km away. Driving averages 60 km/h before parking time. What change is needed?
options: Keep the plan because 60 km can always be driven in 30 minutes.
Delete the distance rather than revise the times.
Allow at least an hour of driving plus a practical arrival buffer.
questions.explanation: At 60 km/h, 60 km requires one hour before parking or delays. The half-hour gap is infeasible; adjust the itinerary and include appropriate buffers.

title: Tourism · Grade 11 · Term 4: Tourism careers and sustainable enterprise · Set A
subject: Tourism

questions.question: Which skill is especially valuable for a tour-planning entrepreneur?
options: Promising every attraction is always open
Copying private customer data without permission
Researching customer needs and building workable costed itineraries
questions.explanation: A viable product needs customer research, realistic logistics, pricing and responsible information handling.

questions.question: Why can tourism businesses benefit from reducing wasted water?
options: It lowers avoidable resource use and can reduce costs
It removes the need for hygiene
It means guests never need drinking water
questions.explanation: Efficiency and conservation support resilience and sustainability. Maintain hygiene and essential services while reducing waste.

questions.question: What does a carbon footprint estimate?
options: Only the size of a person's shoes
Greenhouse gas emissions associated with an activity, usually expressed as CO₂ equivalent
The number of trees in a brochure
A guarantee that an activity has no impact
questions.explanation: A footprint helps identify major emission sources and assess reductions. It depends on boundaries and calculation assumptions.

questions.question: A community starts a guided walking tour. What most supports responsible growth?
options: Excluding local voices from all decisions
Fair local participation, safety planning and protection of places visited
questions.explanation: Responsible enterprise balances economic opportunity with community rights, safety and environmental and cultural care.

questions.question: A walking-tour project doubles visitor numbers while residents report crowding and damage. Which growth plan is strongest?
options: Double visitors again because numbers alone define success.
Ignore residents because tourists are the only stakeholders.
Review carrying capacity, resident feedback and site protection alongside income.
Stop recording damage to improve the statistics.
questions.explanation: Responsible enterprise evaluates visitor benefits with local wellbeing and conservation. Limits, scheduling and community input can protect the asset on which long-term tourism depends.

title: Tourism · Grade 12 · Term 2: World time zones, icons and currency · Set A
subject: Tourism

questions.question: Cape Town is UTC+2 and London is UTC+0 for this question. When it is 14:00 in Cape Town, what time is it in London?
questions.explanation: Subtract the two-hour difference when moving from UTC+2 to UTC+0. Use the offsets provided; daylight-saving rules can differ by date.

questions.question: A flight leaves Johannesburg at 20:00 (UTC+2), lasts 8 hours and lands in a city at UTC+0. Find local arrival time.
questions.explanation: Departure is 18:00 UTC. Add 8 hours to get 02:00 UTC the next day, which is also destination local time.

questions.question: Why is the Eiffel Tower called a tourism icon?
options: It is the only attraction in France
Every icon must be a natural feature
It is widely recognised and associated with its destination
An icon has no marketing value
questions.explanation: An icon is a recognisable symbol or attraction associated with a place. Its reputation can support destination awareness, though visitors have varied interests.

questions.question: A tourist buys €200 at R21 per euro, ignoring fees. What is the rand cost?
questions.explanation: Multiply foreign currency by rand per unit: 200×21=R4 200. Check the appropriate rate and fees for a real transaction.

questions.question: A flight leaves Johannesburg at 23:00 UTC+2, lasts 9 hours and arrives in a city at UTC−5. Which local arrival is correct, using only these offsets?
questions.explanation: Departure is 21:00 UTC. Nine hours later is 06:00 UTC the next day; subtract five hours for the destination to obtain 01:00. Track both offset and date.

title: Tourism · Grade 12 · Term 3: Responsible tourism, heritage and service · Set A
subject: Tourism

questions.question: A hotel offers local jobs but pollutes the river. How should its sustainability be assessed?
options: Jobs prove it is sustainable in every respect
Consider the economic benefit alongside environmental and social harms
questions.explanation: The three pillars must be considered together. Economic benefits do not cancel environmental damage without addressing it.

questions.question: Why consult communities when managing a heritage site?
options: Their knowledge, rights and interests are central to responsible management
Consultation guarantees agreement on every issue
questions.explanation: Participation improves legitimacy and interpretation. Manage differing interests transparently rather than assuming tourism overrides local needs.

questions.question: Which method provides structured customer feedback?
options: A clear post-visit survey with relevant questions
questions.explanation: A survey can collect comparable feedback. Include different guests, consider response bias and use findings to make improvements.

questions.question: Why should a tourism employee understand their employment contract?
options: It sets out duties, terms and relevant employment conditions
It replaces every applicable labour law
It removes all responsibilities from both parties
questions.explanation: A contract helps clarify expectations. Its terms must be considered within the applicable legal framework and should be understood before agreement.

questions.question: A hotel reports 95% satisfaction from a survey offered only to repeat guests. Which evaluation is sound?
options: It proves 95% of every possible guest is satisfied.
Repeat guests always provide unbiased national tourism data.
The result describes respondents but may not represent first-time or dissatisfied guests.
Surveys cannot provide any useful service evidence.
questions.explanation: The sampling method can exclude dissatisfied guests who never return. Include a broader guest sample and examine response rates before generalising the result.

title: Tourism · Grade 12 · Term 4: Integrated travel and destination revision · Set A
subject: Tourism

questions.question: A city is UTC−5 and Johannesburg UTC+2. When it is 18:00 in Johannesburg, what time is it in the other city using these offsets?
questions.explanation: The offset difference is seven hours. Johannesburg is ahead, so subtract seven hours: 18:00−7=11:00.

questions.question: A tour costs R1 500 before a 10% discount. Find the discounted price.
questions.explanation: Discount = 1 500×0.10=R150. Subtract it to get R1 350. The discount amount is not the final price.

questions.question: A guide learns that an attraction is temporarily closed. What is the best response?
options: Verify details, inform travellers and offer a suitable revised itinerary
Keep selling the unchanged itinerary without disclosure
Invent a reason that cannot be checked
Leave travellers stranded at the gate
questions.explanation: Good service uses accurate current information and practical alternatives. Explain material changes clearly before the visit where possible.

questions.question: What makes a destination-marketing claim credible?
options: Unverified awards and invented visitor counts
Specific accurate claims supported by current evidence
A promise that every visitor will have identical experiences
questions.explanation: Evidence, current details and honest scope support informed choices. Marketing should match the experience and resources actually available.

questions.question: A tour costing R1 500 offers 10% off, then charges a R200 booking fee. A competitor offers R1 450 all-inclusive for identical services. Which stated total is lower?
options: The discounted tour's R1 350 because fees do not count.
The competitor's R1 450; the discounted tour totals R1 550.
The first tour costs R1 200 after adding the fee.
questions.explanation: Discounted base price is 1 500×0.9=R1 350; adding R200 gives R1 550. Compare complete prices and equivalent services rather than the headline discount alone.

title: Life Orientation · Grade 10 · Term 2: Civic responsibility and study skills · Set A
subject: Life Orientation

questions.question: A class identifies unsafe litter near its school. What is a constructive civic response?
options: Burn all waste without permission or safety checks
Investigate safely and work with the school and relevant local services on a plan
questions.explanation: Civic participation combines evidence, safe action and cooperation. Define the problem, agree responsibilities and evaluate the outcome.

questions.question: Which study method best checks understanding?
options: Close the notes, explain the idea and answer a practice question
Read the same page without testing recall
Study only the night before every test
questions.explanation: Retrieval and explanation reveal gaps. Check answers and revisit the parts you cannot yet explain accurately.

questions.question: Why evaluate a social-media claim before sharing it?
options: Unverified claims can mislead people and harm others
Sharing is evidence that a claim is true
questions.explanation: Check the original source, date, evidence and context. Avoid amplifying a claim simply because it is emotional or widely repeated.

questions.question: A study plan has five hours without breaks after a full school day. What is a useful improvement?
options: Remove sleep to fit more work
Use manageable focused sessions with breaks and realistic priorities
Treat a missed session as failure of the whole year
questions.explanation: A sustainable plan considers attention, rest, tasks and available time. Review and adapt it rather than demanding an unrealistic schedule.

questions.question: A class shares a dramatic litter-related health claim with no source to encourage cleanup. Which revision best supports responsible civic action?
options: Keep the unverified claim because good intentions guarantee accuracy.
Add more alarming wording instead of checking it.
Verify the claim and communicate accurate evidence alongside a safe cleanup plan.
Ask learners to handle unknown hazardous waste without supervision.
questions.explanation: Responsible action combines credible information with safety and appropriate support. A useful goal does not make an unsupported claim reliable or justify unsafe handling of waste.

title: Life Orientation · Grade 10 · Term 3: Life roles, relationships and careers · Set A
subject: Life Orientation

questions.question: A learner balances schoolwork, family duties and sport. What is a useful first step when demands clash?
options: List priorities, discuss constraints and agree a workable schedule
Assume every demand can happen at the same time
Give up every long-term goal immediately
questions.explanation: Life roles can compete for time. Planning and respectful discussion help negotiate realistic responsibilities and support.

questions.question: What is assertive communication?
options: Expressing needs clearly and respectfully while respecting others' rights
questions.explanation: Assertiveness differs from aggression and passivity. It combines clarity, boundaries and respect.

questions.question: Why research several careers before choosing school-to-work pathways?
options: Entry requirements, tasks and opportunities differ
questions.explanation: Compare reliable information about qualifications, costs, daily work and opportunities with interests and strengths. Keep alternatives open.

questions.question: A friend pressures a learner to ignore an agreed boundary. Which response is healthiest?
options: Assume discomfort must always be ignored
State the boundary clearly and seek trusted support if pressure continues
questions.explanation: Healthy relationships respect consent and boundaries. Support from a trusted adult or professional can help when pressure or harm persists.

questions.question: A learner's career plan conflicts with family duties and transport limits. Which decision process is strongest?
options: Choose solely by a career title's popularity.
Ignore all constraints because motivation removes them.
Compare pathways and requirements, discuss support and make a feasible schedule with alternatives.
Abandon all goals without investigating options.
questions.explanation: A sound plan integrates interests with practical requirements and available support. Comparing alternatives and discussing constraints can identify workable routes rather than treating barriers as either irrelevant or final.

title: Life Orientation · Grade 10 · Term 4: Lifelong learning, diversity and ethical sport · Set A
subject: Life Orientation

questions.question: Why does lifelong learning matter as work changes?
options: One qualification guarantees unchanged work forever
People may need to update skills and adapt to new opportunities
questions.explanation: Technology and economic change can alter tasks and skills. Ongoing learning can support adaptation, although it cannot guarantee employment.

questions.question: What is a respectful response to different religious beliefs at school?
options: Discuss differences without discrimination and respect others' rights
Exclude people from learning because of belief
questions.explanation: A diverse society needs respectful participation and protection of rights. Disagreement does not justify discrimination or harassment.

questions.question: Why is match-fixing unethical?
options: It improves fairness for all participants
It is the same as training harder
It affects only the colour of uniforms
It undermines fair competition and trust in sporting results
questions.explanation: Manipulating results for improper advantage harms players, supporters and the integrity of sport.

questions.question: What should a learner check when investigating a qualification?
options: Its recognition, entry requirements, costs and suitable study pathway
Whether a stranger promises a guaranteed job
Only how quickly a payment can be made
questions.explanation: Use reliable institution and qualification information. Verify legitimacy and requirements before committing time or money.

questions.question: A training advert promises a recognised qualification but names no awarding body. What should a learner do before paying?
options: Pay immediately because attractive branding proves recognition.
Assume every online course has identical recognition.
Verify the provider and qualification through credible official channels and compare the terms.
Use only testimonials supplied by the seller.
questions.explanation: Recognition, provider legitimacy, costs and entry requirements need independent checking. Promotional testimonials and presentation alone cannot establish the status or value of a qualification.

title: Life Orientation · Grade 11 · Term 2: Power relations and environmental responsibility · Set A
subject: Life Orientation

questions.question: Which action helps challenge unequal power in a school group?
options: Give members safe ways to speak and respond fairly to concerns
questions.explanation: Fair participation and accountability can reduce harmful power imbalances. Address intimidation through appropriate school support processes.

questions.question: A learner hears a disclosure of gender-based violence. What is a supportive response?
options: Share the story publicly without consent
Promise to investigate alone through confrontation
Listen without blame and help access trusted, appropriate support
questions.explanation: Support begins with listening, safety and appropriate help. Avoid blame, gossip or actions that may increase risk.

questions.question: Why can environmental pollution become a public-health issue?
options: People can be exposed through air, water or food
questions.explanation: Exposure pathways and pollutant types influence risk. Investigate evidence and use appropriate authorities rather than making unsupported health claims.

questions.question: Which community action supports responsible citizenship?
options: Report illegal dumping through suitable channels and help plan safe prevention
questions.explanation: Responsible action uses safe, lawful channels and cooperation. Prevention should address causes and include affected people.

questions.question: A school committee invites everyone but only senior members can speak safely without ridicule. Which improvement addresses the power imbalance?
options: Treat the invitation alone as proof of equal influence.
Remove the right to raise concerns.
Set respectful discussion rules, safe reporting routes and meaningful participation for less-powerful members.
Allow ridicule so only confident members contribute.
questions.explanation: Formal access does not guarantee equitable voice. Safe processes, responsive leadership and meaningful participation help address how power is exercised in practice.

title: Life Orientation · Grade 11 · Term 3: Lifestyle choices and career competence · Set A
subject: Life Orientation

questions.question: A learner is sleeping too little to keep studying longer. What is the most constructive response?
options: Assume less sleep always improves memory
Use unverified substances to stay awake
Adjust the plan to include rest and seek support with workload
questions.explanation: Rest supports attention and learning. A realistic schedule and timely support are more sustainable than repeated exhaustion.

questions.question: Which is a transferable work skill?
options: Communicating clearly and collaborating on tasks
Memorising one person's phone number only
questions.explanation: Transferable skills can be used across roles and settings. Learners can develop them through projects, responsibilities and reflection.

questions.question: A job advertisement requires a skill the learner has not yet developed. What is a useful next step?
options: Identify credible training and practise the skill while checking other requirements
Assume every training advert is legitimate
Pay anyone promising a guaranteed job
questions.explanation: Compare the gap with reliable training options and develop evidence of competence. Honest applications protect credibility.

questions.question: What does work ethics include?
options: Reliability, honesty and respect for responsibilities
questions.explanation: Ethical conduct involves accountability and consideration of others. Ask for help and correct errors rather than hiding them.

questions.question: A learner's longer study hours reduce sleep and practice-test performance. Which revision best uses the evidence?
options: Add more late-night hours regardless of the results.
Rebalance focused study and rest, review errors and seek support with workload.
Stop reviewing performance because the plan is already written.
questions.explanation: A plan should respond to outcomes and wellbeing. Shorter focused sessions, rest and targeted error review can be evaluated through subsequent progress rather than equating hours alone with learning.

title: Life Orientation · Grade 11 · Term 4: Human rights, moral reasoning and exam planning · Set A
subject: Life Orientation

questions.question: How can a class discuss a moral disagreement constructively?
options: Clarify values, consider evidence and respect people while evaluating ideas
Assume one slogan resolves all dilemmas
questions.explanation: Reasoned discussion distinguishes claims, values and consequences. Respect does not prevent careful criticism of an argument.

questions.question: A learner rereads notes but struggles in tests. What is a useful change?
options: Practise retrieval and timed questions, then review errors
questions.explanation: Practice reveals what can be recalled and applied under test conditions. Feedback helps target the next study session.

questions.question: Why should a study plan be revised after a practice test?
options: The original plan must never change
Errors provide evidence about what needs more attention
questions.explanation: Use mistakes diagnostically: identify the concept, practise it and check again. A score is information about that attempt, not a fixed label.

questions.question: What supports a harmonious multi-religious school community?
options: Excluding minority views from all activities
Stereotyping every member of a religion
Equal dignity, respectful dialogue and fair participation
questions.explanation: Respect for rights supports coexistence amid differences. Policies should protect participation and avoid discrimination.

questions.question: Two study plans use equal hours: one rereads all topics; the other uses error analysis and timed practice. How should effectiveness be evaluated?
options: Count page colours as the sole measure.
Assume equal hours guarantee equal understanding.
Compare progress on relevant practice tasks and adjust for remaining weaknesses.
Choose the plan with the longest title.
questions.explanation: Study effectiveness depends on learning outcomes, not hours alone. Relevant retrieval and application tasks reveal whether understanding and exam performance improve and where further attention is needed.

title: Life Orientation · Grade 12 · Term 2: Media literacy, rights and civic participation · Set A
subject: Life Orientation

questions.question: A news post shows a dramatic claim without a date or source. What should a learner do before sharing?
options: Share because the headline is emotional
Verify the original source, date, context and supporting evidence
Replace verification with the number of likes
questions.explanation: Media literacy includes source evaluation and context. Old or altered material can mislead even when it appears convincing.

questions.question: Why is freedom of expression linked to responsibility?
options: It permits any harassment without consequence
It means only one view may exist
Expression can affect others' rights and requires consideration of lawful limits and harm
It removes every duty to check facts
questions.explanation: Rights operate alongside other rights and responsibilities. Use accurate information and respectful debate rather than threats or discrimination.

questions.question: Which is meaningful participation in a local environmental issue?
options: Assume a viral post alone solves the problem
Gather reliable information, consult affected people and engage relevant decision-makers
questions.explanation: Effective participation combines evidence, inclusion and follow-through. Evaluate whether actions lead to practical changes.

questions.question: How can media representation reinforce stereotypes?
options: Repeated narrow portrayals can make unfair generalisations seem normal
Every repeated portrayal is automatically accurate
Representation has no effect on audiences
questions.explanation: Analyse whose voices appear, who is omitted and how groups are framed. Compare portrayals with varied evidence and lived experiences.

questions.question: A dated photograph is reposted as evidence of an event happening today. Which response best demonstrates media literacy?
options: Treat repeated reposts as independent confirmation.
Assume an emotional caption establishes the date.
Find the original image and date, compare the claimed context and share only verified information.
Share first and check only if challenged.
questions.explanation: Images can be authentic yet misleadingly recaptioned. Tracing provenance and checking time, place and independent evidence tests whether the image supports the current claim.

questions.question: Before accepting a job, what should a learner clarify?

Whether the employer avoids every written record
Duties, pay, hours, conditions and the legitimacy of the employer

questions.question: Why is equity different from treating everyone identically?
options: Equity requires identical support regardless of need
Fair access may require addressing different barriers and support needs
questions.explanation: Equity focuses on fair opportunity and participation, which may involve targeted support or accommodation.

questions.question: A worker notices a safety hazard outside their training. What is the responsible response?
options: Report it through appropriate channels and avoid unsafe untrained action
questions.explanation: Safety includes recognising limits, following procedures and alerting responsible people. Work ethic does not require taking avoidable risks.

questions.question: What is a sound response to a request to falsify a workplace record?
options: Change it because instructions remove responsibility
Refuse falsification and seek appropriate guidance or reporting support
Ask a friend to invent the details
questions.explanation: Honesty and accountability apply even under pressure. Use suitable procedures and support while considering personal safety and context.

questions.question: A learner receives a job offer that omits hours and duties but demands an immediate unexplained payment. What is the strongest next step?
options: Pay immediately because urgency proves legitimacy.
Provide false qualifications to secure the position.
Verify the employer and written terms through independent channels before committing or paying.
Ignore missing conditions because a job title is sufficient.
questions.explanation: Unclear terms and unexplained upfront charges require scrutiny. Independent verification and clear written conditions support an informed decision without treating every offer as automatically genuine.

title: Life Orientation · Grade 12 · Term 4: Post-school planning and exam preparation · Set A
subject: Life Orientation

questions.question: Why should a matric learner prepare more than one post-school option?
options: A first choice is guaranteed once imagined
Admission, funding and opportunities may be uncertain
questions.explanation: A practical plan includes preferred and alternative routes, verified requirements, deadlines and funding options.

questions.question: What belongs on an honest entry-level CV?
options: Relevant education, skills and experience described accurately
A guaranteed salary demand presented as a qualification
questions.explanation: School projects, volunteering and responsibilities can provide relevant evidence. Describe actual contributions and obtain permission for references where appropriate.

questions.question: A learner loses marks despite knowing the content. What should they review?
options: Instruction words, time allocation and how answers address the question
questions.explanation: Exam technique complements knowledge. Practise interpreting commands, structuring answers and allocating time, then use feedback to improve.

questions.question: Why record bursary and application deadlines in a plan?
options: A reminder automatically submits an application
Different opportunities have different requirements and closing dates
questions.explanation: Track exact deadlines and required documents, and verify the official notice. Planning and reminders support action but do not replace submitting a complete application.

questions.question: A learner has one university application and no confirmed funding. Which revised plan best manages uncertainty?
options: Assume application automatically guarantees admission and funding.
Use one deadline for every institution and bursary.
Add suitable alternative study or training pathways and track separate admission and funding requirements.
Wait until all opportunities close before reviewing options.
questions.explanation: Admission and funding are separate, uncertain processes. Realistic alternatives, verified requirements and distinct deadlines reduce the risk of having no workable post-school option.

title: English HL · Grade 10 · Term 2: Reading for evidence and inference · Set A
subject: English HL

questions.question: Where does Mila arrive?
questions.explanation: The first sentence states the location directly. A retrieval question asks for information explicitly present in the text.
questions.stimulus: Mila reached the library after the lights had been switched off. She looked at the book in her hand, then at the locked door. Tomorrow's test suddenly felt much closer.

questions.question: Which detail most clearly shows that she cannot enter?
questions.explanation: The locked door is direct evidence that entry is blocked. The book and test explain her purpose but do not themselves prevent entry.
questions.stimulus: Mila reached the library after the lights had been switched off. She looked at the book in her hand, then at the locked door. Tomorrow's test suddenly felt much closer.

questions.question: What can reasonably be inferred about Mila?
options: She has already written the test
She is concerned about preparing for the test
She is certain she will fail
questions.explanation: The final sentence suggests anxiety about limited preparation time. It does not establish her eventual result.
questions.stimulus: Mila reached the library after the lights had been switched off. She looked at the book in her hand, then at the locked door. Tomorrow's test suddenly felt much closer.

questions.question: Which statement is an unsupported addition to the passage?
options: A test is scheduled for tomorrow
questions.explanation: The passage never gives the test result. An inference must remain within what evidence reasonably supports.
questions.stimulus: Mila reached the library after the lights had been switched off. She looked at the book in her hand, then at the locked door. Tomorrow's test suddenly felt much closer.

questions.question: How does the final sentence affect the reader's understanding of the locked door?
options: It proves Mila has already failed the test.
It shows the library has no books.
It turns a practical obstacle into a moment of increased test anxiety.
It establishes that the test date was changed.
questions.explanation: The test feeling closer links the closed library to Mila's urgency. This emotional effect is supported, whereas a result, missing books or changed date is never stated.
questions.stimulus: Mila reached the library after the lights had been switched off. She looked at the book in her hand, then at the locked door. Tomorrow's test suddenly felt much closer.

title: English HL · Grade 10 · Term 3: Persuasive language and audience · Set A
subject: English HL

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the text?
options: To report a completed sports match
To persuade people to join a reading circle
To provide a formal exam timetable
questions.explanation: The invitation, command and positive promise encourage participation. Purpose concerns what the writer wants the audience to do or think.
questions.stimulus: Join our Saturday reading circle. Bring one book and leave with a hundred ideas! Everyone is welcome, whether you read quickly or take your time.

questions.question: Which expression is a clear exaggeration?
questions.explanation: The large promise emphasises benefit rather than giving a measured count. This hyperbole adds persuasive energy.
questions.stimulus: Join our Saturday reading circle. Bring one book and leave with a hundred ideas! Everyone is welcome, whether you read quickly or take your time.

questions.question: What is the effect of whether you read quickly or take your time?
options: It gives an exact reading-speed statistic
It changes Saturday into a school day
It reassures readers with different reading speeds
questions.explanation: The inclusive wording reduces a possible barrier to joining. Explain the effect with reference to the particular audience.
questions.stimulus: Join our Saturday reading circle. Bring one book and leave with a hundred ideas! Everyone is welcome, whether you read quickly or take your time.

questions.question: Which verb begins an imperative in the text?
questions.explanation: Join directly urges the reader to act. Imperatives commonly omit the subject you, which is understood.
questions.stimulus: Join our Saturday reading circle. Bring one book and leave with a hundred ideas! Everyone is welcome, whether you read quickly or take your time.

questions.question: Is a hundred ideas best read as a precise promise? Choose the strongest evaluation.
options: Yes; every participant is guaranteed exactly one hundred ideas.
No; the phrase proves that no ideas will be shared.
No; the exaggeration enthusiastically promotes the circle rather than measuring an exact outcome.
Yes; a precise attendance count is given.
questions.explanation: The rounded, extravagant number supports persuasive enthusiasm. The passage provides no counting method or guarantee, so treating it as a literal measured promise overstates the evidence.
questions.stimulus: Join our Saturday reading circle. Bring one book and leave with a hundred ideas! Everyone is welcome, whether you read quickly or take your time.

subject: English HL

questions.question: Which phrase uses personification?
questions.explanation: Sleeping is attributed to the classroom, giving an inanimate place a human action and creating a quiet, neglected atmosphere.
questions.stimulus: The classroom slept beneath a blanket of dust. At the window, one small plant leaned towards the sun. Lindi watered it before opening her exercise book.

questions.question: What does a blanket of dust suggest?
options: Someone left a literal wool blanket
questions.explanation: The metaphor compares a covering of dust to a blanket. Interpret its effect rather than treating it as a literal object.
questions.stimulus: The classroom slept beneath a blanket of dust. At the window, one small plant leaned towards the sun. Lindi watered it before opening her exercise book.

questions.question: Which detail shows an act of care?
options: The classroom is described as sleeping
questions.explanation: Watering the plant is a deliberate action that supports its life. This provides evidence for character interpretation.
questions.stimulus: The classroom slept beneath a blanket of dust. At the window, one small plant leaned towards the sun. Lindi watered it before opening her exercise book.

questions.question: Which theme is most supportable from the short passage?
options: Small acts of care amid neglect
questions.explanation: The dusty setting contrasts with Lindi's care for the living plant. A theme must be grounded in the actual details.
questions.stimulus: The classroom slept beneath a blanket of dust. At the window, one small plant leaned towards the sun. Lindi watered it before opening her exercise book.

questions.question: Which evaluation best explains the effect of placing Lindi's action after the dust imagery?
options: The watering proves the classroom has never been used.
The dust establishes that Lindi dislikes all plants.
The small act of watering offers a contrast to the room's apparent neglect.
The sequence proves every other learner is careless.
questions.explanation: The blanket of dust suggests neglect, while watering sustains a living plant. Their juxtaposition creates a meaningful contrast without establishing everyone's motives.
questions.stimulus: The classroom slept beneath a blanket of dust. At the window, one small plant leaned towards the sun. Lindi watered it before opening her exercise book.

subject: English HL

questions.question: What contrast is introduced by yet?
options: The survey happened before the school existed
Longer opening hours did not lead to much higher attendance
questions.explanation: Yet signals an unexpected outcome compared with the likely expectation that more hours would increase use.
questions.stimulus: The school extended library hours, yet attendance barely changed. In a survey, many learners said the last taxi left before closing time. Access, the librarian realised, was more than an unlocked door.

questions.question: Which factor limits access according to the survey?
questions.explanation: Learners identify the last taxi's departure as a constraint. Attribute the claim to the survey rather than inventing unrelated causes.
questions.stimulus: The school extended library hours, yet attendance barely changed. In a survey, many learners said the last taxi left before closing time. Access, the librarian realised, was more than an unlocked door.

questions.question: Which summary preserves the main point most accurately?
options: Longer library hours alone did not solve access because transport remained a barrier.
questions.explanation: A sound summary selects the central relationship without adding unsupported certainty or detail.
questions.stimulus: The school extended library hours, yet attendance barely changed. In a survey, many learners said the last taxi left before closing time. Access, the librarian realised, was more than an unlocked door.

questions.question: What does an unlocked door represent in the final sentence?
options: Proof that all learners can attend
An instruction to remove the door
A narrow idea of access based only on physical opening
questions.explanation: The image highlights the difference between formal availability and practical access. Transport makes the distinction meaningful.
questions.stimulus: The school extended library hours, yet attendance barely changed. In a survey, many learners said the last taxi left before closing time. Access, the librarian realised, was more than an unlocked door.

questions.question: Which judgement best captures the effectiveness of the final image of an unlocked door?
options: It proves the librarian wants fewer learners to attend.
It argues that buildings should never be unlocked.
It exposes the gap between physical opening and learners' practical ability to attend.
It replaces all transport evidence with an unrelated image.
questions.explanation: The door stands for physical availability, but the taxi evidence reveals a further barrier. The final image condenses the argument that access involves more than opening hours.
questions.stimulus: The school extended library hours, yet attendance barely changed. In a survey, many learners said the last taxi left before closing time. Access, the librarian realised, was more than an unlocked door.

title: English HL · Grade 11 · Term 3: Advertising claims and critical literacy · Set A
subject: English HL

questions.question: Which word creates an unjustifiably exclusive claim?
questions.explanation: Only excludes all other routes to success. The passage provides no evidence for such a broad claim.
questions.stimulus: Our study app is the only path to success, says a poster. Beneath the slogan, three smiling learners hold certificates. No results data or comparison is provided.

questions.question: What persuasive function do the smiling learners mainly serve?
options: They associate the app with positive outcomes and satisfaction
They provide the missing results dataset
questions.explanation: Visual endorsement can create positive associations. It does not by itself establish effectiveness or causation.
questions.stimulus: Our study app is the only path to success, says a poster. Beneath the slogan, three smiling learners hold certificates. No results data or comparison is provided.

questions.question: What evidence would best help evaluate the claim?
options: Reliable results with clear methods and an appropriate comparison
questions.explanation: Evidence needs to address the claim, including how outcomes were measured and compared. Design and context matter.
questions.stimulus: Our study app is the only path to success, says a poster. Beneath the slogan, three smiling learners hold certificates. No results data or comparison is provided.

questions.question: Which revision makes the slogan more defensible?
options: No effort needed for top marks
A study tool designed to support your preparation
questions.explanation: The revised wording describes intended support without unsupported guarantees or dismissing other learning routes.
questions.stimulus: Our study app is the only path to success, says a poster. Beneath the slogan, three smiling learners hold certificates. No results data or comparison is provided.

questions.question: Would replacing only path with a useful tool solve every credibility problem? Choose the best answer.
options: Yes; modest wording makes all performance claims automatically true.
No; all advertising is necessarily false.
It reduces the absolute claim, but claims of effectiveness still need evidence.
Yes; smiling faces are sufficient results data.
questions.explanation: A qualified slogan is more defensible than an exclusive guarantee, yet the text still supplies no comparison or results. Wording and evidential support are separate aspects of credibility.
questions.stimulus: Our study app is the only path to success, says a poster. Beneath the slogan, three smiling learners hold certificates. No results data or comparison is provided.

title: English HL · Grade 11 · Term 4: Narrative perspective and imagery · Set A
subject: English HL

questions.question: Who narrates the passage?
questions.explanation: I and my indicate first-person narration. The passage does not give direct access to every character's thoughts.
questions.stimulus: I kept Father's old watch in a drawer. It no longer told the time, but each evening its silence seemed louder. When my sister asked for it, I closed the drawer gently.

questions.question: What does its silence seemed louder suggest?
options: The watch is literally ringing louder
The narrator has measured sound levels
The watch's emotional significance is strongly felt despite its silence
questions.explanation: The apparent contradiction conveys emotional intensity. Explain the contextual effect rather than insisting on a literal sound.
questions.stimulus: I kept Father's old watch in a drawer. It no longer told the time, but each evening its silence seemed louder. When my sister asked for it, I closed the drawer gently.

questions.question: Why should the narrator's motive for closing the drawer remain qualified?
options: The text states every thought explicitly
A first-person narrator can never be interpreted
The sister has already explained it
The action suggests attachment but does not state the full motive
questions.explanation: Inference can identify possibilities supported by details while recognising that the narrator leaves some meaning unstated.
questions.stimulus: I kept Father's old watch in a drawer. It no longer told the time, but each evening its silence seemed louder. When my sister asked for it, I closed the drawer gently.

questions.question: Which response gives the strongest textual support for attachment?
options: Keeping the old watch and reacting to its silence suggest lasting emotional value.
The narrator must be a watchmaker.
The sister definitely plans to sell it.
questions.explanation: The response links a claim to two details and avoids unsupported assumptions about occupation or intentions.
questions.stimulus: I kept Father's old watch in a drawer. It no longer told the time, but each evening its silence seemed louder. When my sister asked for it, I closed the drawer gently.

questions.question: Which evaluation best explains why gently matters in the closing action?
options: It proves the narrator has agreed to give the watch away.
It establishes the watch's exact financial value.
It supports a careful, emotionally weighted response without proving the narrator's full motive.
It shows that the drawer is broken.
questions.explanation: The manner of closing contributes to tone and suggests care or restraint. It enriches the attachment reading but does not state a final decision or a complete motive.
questions.stimulus: I kept Father's old watch in a drawer. It no longer told the time, but each evening its silence seemed louder. When my sister asked for it, I closed the drawer gently.

title: English HL · Grade 12 · Term 2: Evaluating evidence and qualified conclusions · Set A
subject: English HL

questions.question: What is the main weakness in the newsletter's causal claim?
options: A higher pass rate can never be measured
Other changes may also explain the higher pass rate
questions.explanation: Without an appropriate comparison, concurrent changes make it difficult to isolate tutoring's effect. This limits the causal claim without proving the programme ineffective.
questions.stimulus: After a school introduced evening tutoring, its pass rate rose. The newsletter credited the programme. However, the year also saw smaller classes and a change in the learners enrolled. The report did not compare similar groups.

questions.question: Which statement is best supported?
options: Tutoring alone caused the entire rise.
Smaller classes had no possible influence.
Every learner benefited by the same amount.
Pass rates rose after tutoring began, but the programme's independent effect is uncertain.
questions.explanation: The cautious conclusion distinguishes sequence and association from established causation.
questions.stimulus: After a school introduced evening tutoring, its pass rate rose. The newsletter credited the programme. However, the year also saw smaller classes and a change in the learners enrolled. The report did not compare similar groups.

questions.question: What role does However play?
options: It introduces a qualification to the preceding explanation
It confirms the causal claim without reservation
questions.explanation: The connector signals contrasting evidence that complicates the initial explanation. Track relationships between sentences, not only individual facts.
questions.stimulus: After a school introduced evening tutoring, its pass rate rose. The newsletter credited the programme. However, the year also saw smaller classes and a change in the learners enrolled. The report did not compare similar groups.

questions.question: Which additional evidence would most strengthen evaluation?
options: A second slogan praising the programme
A well-designed comparison accounting for class size and learner differences
More copies of the same newsletter
A promise to avoid collecting data
questions.explanation: Comparable groups and attention to alternative explanations help test the claim. No single method removes every limitation, so assess design quality.
questions.stimulus: After a school introduced evening tutoring, its pass rate rose. The newsletter credited the programme. However, the year also saw smaller classes and a change in the learners enrolled. The report did not compare similar groups.

questions.question: Which replacement for the newsletter's claim best preserves the evidence while correcting its overreach?
options: Tutoring alone certainly caused the improvement.
Tutoring had no effect because other things changed.
Pass rates rose after tutoring began, although other changes prevent isolating its effect here.
Smaller classes alone certainly explain every result.
questions.explanation: The passage supports the sequence and the higher pass rate, but not the independent contribution of any change. A sound revision qualifies causation without replacing it with another unsupported certainty.
questions.stimulus: After a school introduced evening tutoring, its pass rate rose. The newsletter credited the programme. However, the year also saw smaller classes and a change in the learners enrolled. The report did not compare similar groups.

title: English HL · Grade 12 · Term 3: Framing, omission and persuasive revision · Set A
subject: English HL

questions.question: What is the effect of Lazy in the headline?
options: It is a neutral measure of motivation
It frames learners negatively before their circumstances are examined
questions.explanation: The loaded label guides judgment without establishing motives. Critical reading separates description from evaluation and evidence.
questions.stimulus: The headline read: Lazy learners abandon the reading room. The article mentioned empty chairs but omitted interviews with learners who lacked evening transport. Its photograph showed a half-empty room taken before opening time.

questions.question: Why does the photograph's timing matter?
options: It may misleadingly suggest low attendance during operating hours
questions.explanation: A pre-opening image is not reliable evidence of attendance while the room operates. Captions and context affect interpretation.
questions.stimulus: The headline read: Lazy learners abandon the reading room. The article mentioned empty chairs but omitted interviews with learners who lacked evening transport. Its photograph showed a half-empty room taken before opening time.

questions.question: Which omission most directly weakens the article's explanation?
questions.explanation: Excluding relevant affected voices can narrow an explanation and conceal practical constraints. The omission matters because it relates directly to attendance.
questions.stimulus: The headline read: Lazy learners abandon the reading room. The article mentioned empty chairs but omitted interviews with learners who lacked evening transport. Its photograph showed a half-empty room taken before opening time.

questions.question: Which headline is more balanced?
options: Reading-room attendance raises questions about access
questions.explanation: The revised headline identifies the issue without assigning unsupported blame. Balanced wording still allows investigation and criticism.
questions.stimulus: The headline read: Lazy learners abandon the reading room. The article mentioned empty chairs but omitted interviews with learners who lacked evening transport. Its photograph showed a half-empty room taken before opening time.

questions.question: Would changing Lazy to absent fully repair the article's fairness? Choose the strongest evaluation.
options: Yes; replacing one word fixes every evidential problem.
No; the learners' transport accounts are irrelevant.
No; the misleading photograph and missing transport accounts would still need correction.
questions.explanation: A less judgemental word reduces loaded framing, but accuracy also depends on representative evidence and image context. The article's problems are connected but not identical.
questions.stimulus: The headline read: Lazy learners abandon the reading room. The article mentioned empty chairs but omitted interviews with learners who lacked evening transport. Its photograph showed a half-empty room taken before opening time.

title: English HL · Grade 12 · Term 4: Close reading and literary argument · Set A

questions.question: Which detail creates the clearest contrast?
options: Noma steps away while others move forward
questions.explanation: The opposing movements foreground Noma's hesitation or different decision. Interpretation should connect this contrast to other details.
questions.stimulus: At the station, Noma unfolded the letter once more. The train arrived, impatient and bright. She put the letter in her pocket and stepped away from the platform's edge, while everyone else moved forward.

questions.question: What does impatient attribute to the train?
options: A measured delay of exactly one hour
A human quality that intensifies urgency
questions.explanation: Personification gives the train urgency and energy, contrasting with Noma's pause. The adjective does not establish a technical fault.
questions.stimulus: At the station, Noma unfolded the letter once more. The train arrived, impatient and bright. She put the letter in her pocket and stepped away from the platform's edge, while everyone else moved forward.

questions.question: Which interpretation remains appropriately qualified?
options: The letter definitely contains a job rejection.
The repeated reading and backward movement suggest uncertainty about departing.
The other travellers know the letter's contents.
questions.explanation: The text supports hesitation but does not reveal the letter's content or full history. A defensible argument respects those limits.
questions.stimulus: At the station, Noma unfolded the letter once more. The train arrived, impatient and bright. She put the letter in her pocket and stepped away from the platform's edge, while everyone else moved forward.

questions.question: Which sentence best integrates evidence into an analytical claim?
options: Noma is sad because all stations are sad.
The train is bright, so the letter is good news.
The passage proves that travel is always harmful.
Noma's movement away as others move forward dramatises her separation from their shared purpose.
questions.explanation: The strongest claim connects a specific textual contrast to an interpreted effect without unsupported universal conclusions.
questions.stimulus: At the station, Noma unfolded the letter once more. The train arrived, impatient and bright. She put the letter in her pocket and stepped away from the platform's edge, while everyone else moved forward.

questions.question: Which evaluation best explains the effect of the train's urgency beside Noma's retreat?
options: It proves the letter orders Noma to leave the country.
It establishes that the train is literally conscious.
The contrast intensifies tension between outward movement and her apparent hesitation.
It proves Noma will never travel again.
questions.explanation: Impatient gives the train human urgency, while Noma steps away as others advance. The contrast supports tension and hesitation without revealing the letter or her eventual decision.
questions.stimulus: At the station, Noma unfolded the letter once more. The train arrived, impatient and bright. She put the letter in her pocket and stepped away from the platform's edge, while everyone else moved forward.

title: Mathematics · Grade 10 · Term 2 selection · Set B: Mixed revision
subject: Mathematics

questions.question: A right triangle has opposite side 3 and hypotenuse 5 for angle θ. What is sin θ?
questions.explanation: Sine is opposite divided by hypotenuse. Identify the sides relative to θ before choosing a ratio.

questions.question: R2 000 earns 8% simple interest each year for 3 years. Find the final amount.
questions.explanation: Interest = 2 000 × 0.08 × 3 = R480. Add the original R2 000; R480 alone is only the interest.

questions.question: Find the nth term of 5, 8, 11, 14, …
questions.explanation: The common difference is 3, so use 3n + c. Setting n = 1 gives c = 2. Check n = 2 gives 8.

questions.question: A cylinder has radius 3 cm and height 5 cm. Find its volume in terms of π.
questions.explanation: Volume = πr²h = π × 3² × 5. Radius is squared; do not use the diameter as the radius.

questions.question: A closed cube is enlarged until its volume is eight times the original. A learner says its surface area also becomes eight times as large. Which correction is justified?
options: Lengths become eight times as large, so area doubles.
Lengths double, so surface area is unchanged.
Lengths double, so surface area becomes four times as large.
Lengths quadruple, so surface area doubles.
questions.explanation: Volume scales with the cube of length: a factor of 8 means lengths double. Area scales with the square, giving a factor of 4, not 8.

title: Mathematical Literacy · Grade 10 · Term 2 selection · Set B: Mixed revision
subject: Mathematical Literacy

questions.question: A learner earns R900 and spends R250 on transport and R400 on food. What remains?
questions.explanation: Total spending = 250+400 = R650. Remaining money = income−spending = 900−650 = R250.

questions.question: A product costs R80 and sells for R100. What is the profit?
questions.explanation: Profit = selling price−cost price = R100−R80 = R20. This is the amount, not a percentage.

questions.question: A class of 40 learners has 10 who walk to school. What angle represents them in a pie chart?
questions.explanation: The fraction is 10/40 = ¼. Multiply by 360° to get 90°. The percentage 25% is not an angle.

questions.question: A bar graph starts its vertical axis at 90 instead of 0. What should you check before comparing bars?
options: Whether every bar becomes a percentage
Whether the data must be false
Whether the shortened scale exaggerates differences
Whether the units can be ignored
questions.explanation: A truncated axis can make small differences look large. Read the scale and values before drawing a conclusion.

questions.question: Two adverts show the same sales rising from 100 to 110. One graph begins at zero; the other at 99. Which judgement is sound?
options: The second graph proves a 110% increase.
The first graph must conceal a fall.
Both can show correct values, but the second can exaggerate the visual increase.
Different axis starts necessarily mean different data.
questions.explanation: The numerical increase is 10/100×100=10% in both. The shortened axis changes visual proportions, so read the actual scale before judging the adverts.

questions.question: A shop offers 20% off R450. What do you pay?

questions.question: A box holds 6 L by its outside dimensions. A buyer needs to store 6 L of liquid and claims it is guaranteed to fit. Which response is justified?
options: The outside volume always equals usable liquid capacity.
Six litres means the box has a 6 m length.
Check internal capacity and usable space; outside dimensions do not guarantee 6 L storage.
questions.explanation: Capacity depends on internal dimensions, wall thickness and any necessary headspace. An external-volume calculation alone does not establish usable storage.

It is lower, so ΔH is negative

questions.question: For Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻, what happens to zinc?

It is oxidised by losing electrons

questions.question: A learner dilutes 100 mL of 0.4 mol·dm⁻³ solution to a final volume of 400 mL and claims the moles become one quarter. Which correction is right?

Both moles and concentration remain unchanged.
Moles remain 0.04 mol; concentration becomes 0.1 mol·dm⁻³.
Adding water creates additional solute moles.
questions.explanation: Initial moles are 0.4×0.100=0.04 mol. Without loss or reaction, dilution changes volume, not solute amount. Final concentration is 0.04/0.400=0.1 mol·dm⁻³.

The temperature change; Boyle's law alone requires constant temperature.
Compression means the number of molecules must halve.
questions.explanation: For a fixed amount of gas, PV/T is constant in the ideal model. Pressure also depends on absolute temperature; warming means the constant-temperature doubling claim is unjustified.

questions.explanation: V=ε−Ir=12−2×1=10 V while supplying current. The internal resistor accounts for the lost volts.

questions.question: A generator converts predominantly which energy into electrical energy?
options: Nuclear energy directly with no process
questions.explanation: Relative motion in a magnetic field induces emf. Mechanical input drives the generator, transferring energy to the electrical circuit.

questions.question: Find the pH of a strong monoprotic acid with [H₃O⁺] = 1 × 10⁻³ mol·dm⁻³.
questions.explanation: pH=−log₁₀[H₃O⁺]=−log₁₀(10⁻³)=3. The minus sign reverses the exponent's sign.

questions.question: For an exothermic forward reaction, increasing temperature shifts equilibrium towards…
questions.explanation: Heat is effectively a product in an exothermic reaction. Increasing temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction, increasing the proportion of reactants.

questions.question: A trolley's momentum changes by 6 kg·m·s⁻¹. Two bumpers produce this same change in 0.1 s and 0.3 s. Which safety argument is justified?
options: The 0.3 s bumper gives three times the average net force.
Both average forces must be equal because impulse is equal.
The 0.3 s bumper gives one third of the average net force.
Longer stopping time must increase the momentum change.
questions.explanation: Average net force is impulse divided by contact time. The same 6 N·s gives 60 N over 0.1 s and 20 N over 0.3 s; longer time lowers the average force.

questions.question: In grass → grasshopper → frog, what is the grasshopper?
questions.explanation: Grass is the producer. The grasshopper eats the producer, so it is the primary consumer; the frog is a secondary consumer.

questions.question: Which scientific name is correctly written in plain text?
questions.explanation: The genus begins with a capital and the species epithet with lowercase. In formatted writing both are italicised, or separately underlined when handwritten.

questions.question: Why are fungi not classified as plants?
options: They obtain organic nutrients rather than photosynthesising like green plants
questions.explanation: Fungi are heterotrophs and absorb nutrients. Their cell walls typically contain chitin, rather than the cellulose characteristic of plants.

questions.question: Which feature is shared by plants and animals?
options: They both have chloroplasts in every cell
They both have cellulose cell walls
questions.explanation: Plants and animals are eukaryotes with membrane-bound nuclei. Animal cells do not have chloroplasts or cellulose walls.

questions.question: A culture of microorganisms grows on dead plant material. A learner calls all of them harmful. Which evaluation is best?
options: Growth on dead material proves every organism causes human disease.
Anything too small to see has no ecological role.
Decomposition may recycle nutrients; identify organisms and effects before classifying harm.
Microorganisms are always beneficial and never pathogenic.
questions.explanation: Microorganisms have diverse roles, including decomposition and disease. The observed nutrient-recycling activity does not support an unrestricted claim that all are harmful.

questions.question: Which organ removes urea from the blood and helps regulate water balance?

questions.question: What happens when ADH secretion increases in a healthy person?
options: Less water is reabsorbed and all urine stops
More water is reabsorbed, usually producing a smaller volume of more concentrated urine

questions.question: A population rises by 15 after 30 births, 20 deaths, 10 immigrants and 5 emigrants. Which prediction about next year is warranted?
options: It must rise by exactly 15 every year.
Births alone guarantee a rise of 30.
No exact prediction follows without next year's rates and conditions.
questions.explanation: The net change describes one interval: 30+10−20−5=15. Future births, deaths, migration and resource limits may differ, so extrapolating the same change as a certainty is unjustified.

subject: Life Sciences

questions.question: A population has inherited variation in beak size. A food change favours larger beaks. What explains larger beaks becoming more common over generations?
options: Every bird consciously enlarges its beak
The environment directly rewrites every bird's genes in the same way
Individuals evolve because they need to survive
Individuals with advantageous inherited traits leave more surviving offspring
questions.explanation: Natural selection acts on existing heritable variation. Changes in reproductive success alter trait frequencies across generations, not by individual intention.

questions.question: Which finding supports an African origin of modern humans?
options: The claim that living humans belong to separate biological races ranked by ability
The claim that evolution stopped outside Africa
Fossil and genetic evidence consistent with early modern humans in Africa and later dispersal
The absence of all fossils outside Africa
questions.explanation: The Out-of-Africa model is supported by multiple lines of fossil and genetic evidence. It does not rank living populations or deny later migration and interbreeding.

questions.question: Why does meiosis contribute to variation?
options: It produces only genetically identical gametes
Crossing over and independent assortment produce different allele combinations
It doubles chromosome number in each gamete
questions.explanation: Crossing over and independent chromosome assortment create different combinations. Meiosis also halves chromosome number for sexual reproduction.

questions.question: A healthy person becomes dehydrated. Which response helps conserve water?
options: Decreased ADH and unlimited water loss
Kidneys stop responding to hormones permanently
Increased ADH and increased kidney water reabsorption
More dilute urine in every circumstance
questions.explanation: Dehydration generally stimulates ADH release, promoting water reabsorption and smaller volumes of concentrated urine.

questions.question: A pesticide kills 95% of insects. Survivors produce offspring that also resist it. What control-study evidence would strengthen an inherited-resistance explanation?
options: Every survivor is assumed to have chosen resistance.
Only the pesticide bottle's colour is recorded.
Resistance persists in offspring raised without pesticide and differs from a susceptible comparison line.
No offspring are tested because survival proves inheritance.
questions.explanation: Raising offspring without exposure helps distinguish inherited resistance from an immediate environmental response. A susceptible comparison and repeated trials strengthen the interpretation.

They must become identical in every feature
They must live on different planets

They prove organisms are the same species
They arise only from identical environments

options: Each bird reports trying harder to grow a beak.
Only the population's location is recorded.
Beak-size variation is inherited and larger-beaked birds leave more surviving offspring.
A single adult changes its posture for a photograph.
questions.explanation: Natural selection requires heritable variation and differential reproductive success. A change in frequency alone needs evidence linking the trait to inheritance and survival or reproduction.

subject: Accounting

questions.question: Sales are R80 000 and cost of sales R50 000. Find gross profit.
questions.explanation: Gross profit = sales−cost of sales = R30 000. Operating expenses are deducted later when calculating net profit.

questions.question: Current assets total R60 000 and current liabilities R30 000. Find the current ratio.
questions.explanation: Current ratio = current assets/current liabilities = 60 000/30 000 = 2:1. It is one indicator of short-term liquidity, not a guarantee of solvency.

questions.question: Direct materials cost R8 000 and direct labour R5 000. Find prime cost.
questions.explanation: Prime cost = direct materials + direct labour = R13 000. Factory overheads are added separately for total production cost.

questions.question: A cash budget opens with R4 000, receives R9 000 and pays R10 000. Find its closing balance.
questions.explanation: Closing cash = opening cash+receipts−payments = 4 000+9 000−10 000 = R3 000. Opening cash must be included.

questions.question: A cash budget shows a R3 000 closing balance after excluding depreciation of R1 000. A learner deducts depreciation again. Which judgement is correct?
options: Reduce cash to R2 000 because every expense is a payment.
Increase cash to R4 000 because depreciation creates cash.
Keep R3 000; depreciation is not a cash payment in this budget.
Treat depreciation as a receipt from customers.
questions.explanation: Depreciation allocates an asset's cost as an expense without a current cash outflow. Deducting it in a cash budget would understate cash; actual asset purchases are considered separately.

Increase output VAT to hide the unsupported claim.

questions.explanation: FIFO issues the oldest units first: 10×20 + 2×30 = R260. The remaining eight units are from the R30 batch.

questions.question: Why separate asset custody from record keeping where practical?
options: To reduce the risk of undetected error or fraud
To make records confidential from auditors
questions.explanation: Segregation of duties makes unauthorised actions harder to conceal. It reduces risk but requires checks and does not eliminate every risk.

questions.question: A company has current assets R300 000 and liabilities due within a year R200 000. Find the current ratio.
questions.explanation: Current ratio = current assets/current liabilities = 300 000/200 000=1.5:1. Assess stock quality and collection timing as well.

questions.question: Why should a bank reconciliation investigate unexplained differences?
options: All differences are automatically bank fraud
Reconciliation changes the bank's actual cash without evidence
A bank statement never contains errors
They may reveal recording errors, timing differences or unauthorised transactions
questions.explanation: Reconciliation compares independent records. Identify and substantiate each difference before recording any necessary correction.

questions.question: A business repays a R40 000 loan and its current ratio worsens. A director calls the repayment an expense that reduced profit. Which evaluation is sound?
options: Principal repayment always reduces profit by R40 000.
Loan principal reduces cash and liabilities; assess liquidity separately from interest expense.
A lower current ratio necessarily proves fraud.
questions.explanation: Repayment of principal reduces an asset and a liability, rather than being an operating expense. Interest is accounted for separately; the remaining cash and liability classification affect liquidity analysis.

Pretend the question was never asked

Which unrelated political party does your family support?
Why should we ignore your skills?
Will you accept unsafe work without questions?

Guarantee the employee never needs support

Treat friendship as proof of occupational competence.

questions.question: A SWOT lists a new competitor as a weakness and poor staff training as a threat. Which correction is justified?

Training is always external and competition always internal.
questions.explanation: SWOT distinguishes internal capabilities from external conditions. A competing firm is external, while the business's own staff-development gap is internal; the distinction guides suitable responses.

title: Economics · Grade 10 · Term 2 selection · Set B: Mixed revision
subject: Economics

questions.question: What is a main benefit of a generally accepted medium of exchange over barter?
options: It reduces the need for a double coincidence of wants
questions.explanation: Money allows people to sell to one person and buy from another without each wanting exactly the other's goods.

questions.question: Which action is part of collective bargaining?
options: A firm hides wages from every worker
A worker guesses the inflation rate
Worker representatives and employers negotiate employment conditions
questions.explanation: Collective bargaining involves representatives negotiating employment matters. Its outcomes depend on the process and applicable framework.

questions.question: Which situation best illustrates structural unemployment?
options: A worker voluntarily takes one lunch break
Workers' skills do not match the jobs available after industry changes
A firm changes its stationery colour
questions.explanation: Structural unemployment involves a mismatch between labour supply and demand, including skills or location. Retraining may be part of a response.

questions.question: Why might public works programmes help address unemployment?
options: They guarantee permanent jobs for everyone
They eliminate the need for training
They can provide temporary paid work and useful infrastructure
questions.explanation: Public works can provide income and assets while broader employment measures develop. Their scale, duration and training content affect their impact.

questions.question: A labour force has 800 employed and 200 unemployed. Fifty unemployed people stop seeking work and leave this defined labour force. What happens to the rate?
options: It stays 20% because population cannot change.
It falls to 0% because all unemployment ended.
It falls to about 15.8%, although no additional person got a job.
It rises to 25% because jobs were created.
questions.explanation: Using the stated labour-force definition, unemployment is now 150 and labour force 950: 150/950≈15.8%. The fall reflects withdrawal rather than job creation, so interpretation matters.

title: Economics · Grade 10 · Term 4 selection · Set B: Mixed revision
subject: Economics

questions.question: If demand rises while supply is unchanged, what happens to equilibrium price in the standard model?
questions.explanation: A rightward demand shift raises equilibrium price and quantity, other things equal. Distinguish a shift from movement along a demand curve.

questions.question: Why do economic choices have opportunity costs?
options: Choosing one option can mean giving up the next best alternative
Money is the only scarce resource
questions.explanation: Scarcity creates trade-offs. Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative forgone, which need not be a cash payment.

questions.question: A country has 40 births and 25 deaths per 1 000 people, ignoring migration. Find its natural increase per 1 000.
questions.explanation: Natural increase = birth rate−death rate = 40−25=15 per 1 000. Migration is a separate component of population change.

questions.question: Why is education relevant to labour productivity?
options: It guarantees every worker a job
It can develop knowledge and skills that improve output per worker
It eliminates differences between all occupations
questions.explanation: Human-capital development can support productivity, alongside health, technology and work organisation. It does not by itself guarantee employment.

questions.question: Training raises output per worker, but employment does not immediately rise. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Training must have failed because employment was unchanged.
Output per worker and worker numbers are the same measure.
Productivity can improve without a simultaneous increase in the number employed.
The result proves training always reduces employment.
questions.explanation: Productivity concerns output relative to inputs, not simply the number of jobs. Demand, investment and business conditions also influence hiring, so separate these indicators when evaluating the programme.

title: Economics · Grade 11 · Term 2 selection · Set B: Mixed revision
subject: Economics

questions.question: Which best distinguishes economic development from economic growth?
options: Growth means only a higher population
Development includes living conditions and structural improvements, beyond output growth
questions.explanation: Growth concerns increased real output. Development considers broader changes such as living standards, capabilities and economic structure.

questions.question: Why do commercial banks assess borrowers before lending?
options: To guarantee no loan can ever default
To remove the need for contracts
To evaluate repayment ability and credit risk
To lend every deposit to one person
questions.explanation: Credit assessment supports prudent lending and risk management, though it cannot eliminate defaults.

questions.question: What is a negative externality of factory air pollution?
options: Only the factory's paid wage bill
A health cost borne by nearby residents that is not fully included in the factory's private costs
A benefit paid directly to every resident
questions.explanation: An external cost affects third parties outside the market transaction. Policy may seek to make decision-makers account for it.

questions.question: Which action supports sustainable resource use?
options: Use every renewable resource faster than it regenerates
Treat pollution as having no cost
Harvest at a rate that allows replenishment while protecting ecosystems
questions.explanation: Sustainability considers current needs, ecosystem limits and future needs. Renewable does not mean unlimited at any rate of use.

questions.question: A factory creates jobs but imposes unpriced health costs on neighbours. Which policy appraisal is strongest?
options: Ignore health costs because they are outside the factory's accounts.
Close every factory without considering alternatives.
Compare employment benefits and external health costs, and assess measures that reduce pollution efficiently.
Treat all private costs as identical to all social costs.
questions.explanation: A negative externality means some costs fall on third parties. A reasoned appraisal considers both benefits and social costs, including the effectiveness and consequences of corrective measures.
